speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, consequent upon a number of complaints of Canadian citizens of Japanese origin who resided in British Columbia in 1941 that their real and personal property had been disposed of by the custodian of alien enemy property at prices less than the fair market value, the government, as soon as possible after the cessation of hostilities, by order in council P.C. 1810 dated July 18, 1947, as amended, appointed Mr. Justice H. I. Bird of the appellate division of the Supreme Court of British Columbia as a royal commissioner under the Inquiries Act to conduct an inquiry. Mr. Justice Bird's report was received in due course and I am tabling it now.
The government will provide compensation totalling $1,222,829.16 in accordance 55946-224i
with those of the commissioner's recommendations which fall within the terms of reference. For this purpose it will bring down, at the present session, a supplementary estimate.
The commissioner also felt it incumbent upon him to deal with several claims which, strictly speaking, were outside the terms of reference and which he has dealt with in sixteen special reports. The government intends to carefully consider these special claims and the commissioner's special reports are before the treasury board for this purpose at the present time. These claims total approximately $150,000.
I wish at this stage publicly to express to Mr. Justice Bird the government's appreciation of the service rendered by him during the two years and four months which he has devoted exclusively to this important work, carried through, as it has been, in the most painstaking and comprehensive manner.
Mr. Justice Bird's report dealt with a total of 1,434 claims relating to residential, farm and business properties; household effects; agricultural tools and equipment; stock in trade and trade fixtures; fishing vessels, gear and nets and motorcars and trucks, which had been vested in the custodian and had been sold by him. These claims related to 7,086 parcels of real and personal property, and involved filing of 8,996 exhibits. After a number of claims had been rejected and withdrawn, the report finally recommends payment to 1,300 Canadians of Japanese origin of various amounts totalling $1,222,829.16.
Having regard to these facts, and also to the difficulties encountered in eliciting the necessary information from many claimants who were not familiar with the English language, the monumental nature of the task with which the commissioner was faced at once becomes apparent. Only his unlimited patience and clear thought have made possible the report which reflects so much credit upon himself.
In his report Mr. Justice Bird makes complimentary references to the good faith and sincerity with which the custodian of alien property discharged his duties. He also pays tribute to the efficient and co-operative manner in which counsel for the claimants and for the commission carried out their duties, and it is quite apparent that without

Inquiries of the Ministry such co-operation, the report which is now being tabled could not have been as good as it is.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it was at my suggestion that this convention was referred to the standing committee on external affairs. As I had expected, the committee gave the matter its usual careful consideration, and has now recommended approval of the convention.
We learned that the world meteorological organization will be a successor to what has been known as the international meteorological organization, which has been functioning for about seventy-five years, and apparently with a considerable measure of success. When I spoke before I expressed some concern about other countries, such as Russia, getting weather information from Canada. It now appears that Canada needs weather information from Siberia, and that Russia needs weather information from western Europe. So that both blocs in the world today require this weather organization, and it is no doubt for that reason that there has been co-operation.
One can only express the hope that it may be possible to convince the two world blocs that they need each other in world affairs generally as well as in connection with weather reports. If they should reach that conclusion, then much of the friction in the world would be removed and the United Nations would be enabled to fulfil its high aim of preserving peace.
I am personally grateful to the committee for giving careful consideration to the convention, and I agree that Canada should join this organization.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I cannot let this opportunity go by without having something to say about apples generally, and especially the apples grown in Ontario, with particular emphasis upon the excellent apples produced in Durham county; and I could include in that category Northumberland county as well. Had the supersalesmen from British Columbia not started peddling their wares and their grievances here last night I should have maintained my sphinx-like silence and allowed the business of the house to continue without interruption. As it is I must leap to the defence of the Ontario apple growers, whose produce throughout the years has been proven to be the finest in Canada.
For a few moments I would like to deal with the importance of the apple in the development of our world. Even in the beginning there were apples, and poor Eve fell victim to their irresistible charm. She knew that the McIntosh red upon which she gazed would have a flavour incomparable

among all the fruits of the earth. She knew that one bite from the apple would make her healthy and wise. Could the devil have tempted her with a sheaf of western wheat, a bunch of grapes, a gold nugget, or a B.C. fir? No; it had to be that most attractive of all things, the apple.
The great law of gravitation was also discovered because of the apple; for when Newton sat under the trees in his orchard and saw one of those apples fall he began to wonder why the apple did not fall upward. Could he have discovered the law of gravitation by looking at a Prince Edward Island potato or the iron ore of Labrador? No; you and I must admit that the apple falling on Newton's head was of great importance in the progress of our world.
In national affairs the apple plays a great part. If you visit a certain town in Italy you will find a most delightful little chapel erected in honour of William Tell, who won his greatest fame because he shot an apple from his son's head. He never could have shot a grape, or a Winnipeg goldeye; therefore the apple all the way round, religion, science, sport and in every other particular, is the greatest of all the fruits, and we owe it an immense debt of gratitude.
Even in our bodies we have the Adam's apple, and -when we talk of a thing of beauty we say "She is the apple of my eye." Why was it the apple was chosen to set forth those delightful, those entrancing, those incomparable qualities and virtues? Because it has within itself the very essence of value.
But I will give you the best proof of all that the apple plays a part in life when everything else fails. You remember King Solomon. He wrote a love poem at one time; and he had a good deal of experience in love. If ever there was a man qualified to write about love it must be King Solomon. You will find at one time that he got very sick of love, and when he desired something that would be a very excellent substitute he wrote this line in his poem: "Stay me with flagons, comfort me with apple, for I am sick of love." You can picture King Solomon with a jug of cider and a plate of apples, and he found that more consolation than all his wives.
I could go on giving example after example of the importance of the apple in our economy and in the health of our nation. Let us never forget the adage that an apple a day keeps the doctor away. I could tell of the versatility of this fruit. You can bake it, boil it, roast it or fry it; serve it with meats, or preserve it, or jam it, or pickle it. You can drink it; you can eat it. It has many

forms and many uses; that is what makes it so wonderful that no other fruit can be compared to it.
For the benefit of those who have listened so patiently, let me bring you up to date on the apple industry in Canada. For the past several years the industry has been flourishing and happy. The growers in Ontario and Quebec have watched the federal government extend financial and marketing assistance to the growers in British Columbia and Nova Scotia, a situation which was satisfactory to the Ontario people because it kept the British Columbia and Nova Scotia apples away from the Ontario market, giving the local producers a good domestic market which in most cases took care of the Ontario crop. To appreciate the picture fairly well it must be explained that in Nova Scotia and British Columbia the growers are confined to small areas compared with Ontario, so it was a comparatively easy matter to have the western and eastern apples packed and shipped or processed through a central agency. Such central agencies made it comparatively simple to distribute subsidies. In Ontario the growers are spread across the province, and it has been very difficult to set up any centralized control and sales organization.
This year an unfortunate event occurred which has left a sour taste in the mouths of the Ontario growers. Production of apples was high and markets were not too plentiful. Many orchardists in Ontario lost a considerable amount of money. One large grower has told me that he lost $40,000 and that a friend of his lost over $20,000. Others just broke even, and a few made costs but not much more. Early in the spring an announcement was made in this house to the effect that $2 million would be given to the British Columbia growers and $500,000 to the growers of Nova Scotia. There was no complaint from the Ontario people, who in many cases had also taken a financial beating. To make matters worse, a few weeks after that announcement, just when Ontario growers normally market their Northern Spies, it was found that British Columbia had been able to sell the large Ontario and Quebec chain stores on a proposal to give exclusive rights to British Columbia apples for a period of several weeks, during which an intensive advertising campaign was conducted in the press, paid for, as I understand it, half by the British Columbia growers and half by the chain stores involved. Needless to say this program literally wiped out the market for Ontario Northern Spies, which had to be held over and sold later or disposed of in other ways. Now we hear the hon. member
S upp ly-A griculture
for Kootenay West bragging how many apples they sold in Ontario and will sell in the future, to which I reply that had the Ontario growers received a $2 million subsidy, they might have been able to sell apples in British Columbia. But Ontario growers have received no subsidy, and find themselves in a grim position at the moment. Even though the subsidies, we are told, definitely will not extend to cover this year's crop of apples, both British Columbia and Nova Scotia have their marketing and packing organizations well established, due in the main to the assistance provided from federal funds. Certainly had it not been for that assistance they would not have been financially able to build up and maintain such organizations. It should also be pointed out that despite this yearly support from federal funds both British Columbia and Nova Scotia have continued planting young trees so that their production is now greater than it was ten years ago. In fact, as I understand it, the entire apple industry in Canada, is now producing about forty per cent more apples than can be consumed under present conditions in Canada.
The future of the industry appears to be precarious. Ontario growers have recommended that the federal government undertake a program of tree removal, in co-operation with the provincial authorities, to decrease the production of apples, but the minister has stated that any such program must be initiated by the province, which would appear to be the logical place for such a project to start. However, I do hope that the minister will continue to give serious consideration to evolving, in co-operation with the growers and the provinces in all of Canada, some method either of stemming production of apples or of increasing the demand for apples through advertising and other means, so that this industry, which is most important to the economy of our country, will again be able to carry on in a selfsustaining manner without the need for annual hand-outs.

speechtext:
In reply to the member who has just spoken, I wish to say that we grow apples in British Columbia, and I sliould like to remind him of the fact that half the Canadian apples are grown in that area. The remainder of Canada-Ontario, Nova Scotia and the other provinces-account for the other half, so that the amount produced in the Okanagan valley equals that produced by the rest of Canada.

I wish to deal briefly with the British market situation. I believe the member for Kootenay West and the member for Kamloops have already outlined our difficulties by showing how the British market constitutes our normal outlet. It is the normal outlet because the industry has grown up around it. I was wondering whether a special effort could not be made to market our apples this year. I noted what the minister said last night that we have to talk a different language. Perhaps that is so, but personally I believe there are other ways of doing it than by talking tough. The only way to do it is to have someone appointed especially to do the job. We send trade commissioners and other representatives to Britain to sell our wheat, bacon, cheese, and so on, and away behind come apples. I should like to see funds taken from one of these items to send a special delegation, appointed by the government and the tree fruit growing areas, to Britain. I am not speaking for our own area alone, but for Canada as a whole.
This delegation could go to the United Kingdom for the sole purpose of trying to sell apples and re-establish this market, not just for this year but for all time to come. As I have pointed out, Britain is buying apples from the other countries, such as Australia and New Zealand. I do believe that if a special delegation, with the strength of the government and the knowledge of the tree fruit board behind it, went to England and remained there until they made some sort of a deal, we would be satisfied. Special instructions should also be issued to the trade commissioners in the various countries to exert themselves to assist the growers in marketing their fruit, and pointing out to them the difficulty in which we find ourselves. I hope it is only temporary. The trade commissioners should be instructed to help the growers of Nova Scotia, Ontario, and all the provinces, to sell their fruit in these various markets.

subtopic: APPROVAL OF CONVENTION OF WORLD METEOROLOGICAL ORGANIZATION SIGNED AT WASHINGTON OCTOBER 11, 1947
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I do not want to leave the committee with the impression that less has been done to sell apples than has been done to sell other products. I venture to say there has been at least ten times as much done abroad to sell apples as needed to be done to sell anything else. We have been unable to sell apples in Great Britain; at least Britain has not wanted to take apples since 1939. We have discussed the matter with them every year to try to obtain a market for apples. When we could not obtain a market we have been called upon to subsidize the apple industry. Our complete subsidies in Nova Scotia have amounted to $18 million; our subsidies in British Columbia have

amounted to $4 million. This has been done in an effort not only to market the apples, but to make it possible for the producers to get a proper return. All the fruit has been marketed in some way or other. At times the apples were canned and given away, and at other times they were dehydrated and given away. We have tried in every way to market apples, and we have succeeded in marketing them. I do not believe the money which has been put into these subsidies has been thrown away. The apple industry is going to be necessary in order to supply the market.
The fact is, as the Minister of Trade and Commerce stated the other day, that right from the beginning of the war Britain said that the freight on apples was too high as compared with the food value of the fruit. During the time the war was in progress there was a shortage of shipping space, and Britain would not take apples at all. It was only at periods when there was shipping space available that they did enter into arrangements with us to take apples. When the war was over it was another problem. They started out as though they intended to take apples; but since then they have got into the position where they are battling with regard to dollars and sterling, and they are just not taking our apples.
I find it difficult to understand even the figures I gave last night. As I understand it, the British Columbia apple producers gave the British about 1,600,000 boxes of apples. They gave away 50,000 boxes, according to the statement from the press that I read to the committee last night. They gave 50,000 boxes to the school children and to the institutions. What did they do with the remainder of them? If they were sold to the people of Britain at the usual price, I just want to ask one question. Who ought to have the returns? I think that is an obvious question. I do not know what was done with the remainder of them, but I think the people of British Columbia who gave the apples ought to know. If they intended them to be an advertisement to the British people, then I think more than 50,000 boxes should have been given arway. If they intended them to be a gift to the British government on which they could make money to put in the treasury well, all right; that is their own affair. There should be some questions asked about it. That is what I meant by talking to these people a little straighter than we sometimes talk. I do not think that the thirteen or fourteen million people of this country should be attempting in peacetime to feed a population of fifty million in a country that is now actually boasting, and I think
Supply-Agriculture
properly boasting, of the extent to which they have rehabilitated their people up to now as compared with other nations of the world.
I do not think that a little bit of straight talking to them is going to do any harm. If we are to go on assuming that the people of this country are to give away everything they have, I do not know where we shall find the people who are going to buy what we have, because people apparently like having things given to them.

subtopic: APPROVAL OF CONVENTION OF WORLD METEOROLOGICAL ORGANIZATION SIGNED AT WASHINGTON OCTOBER 11, 1947
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I was at a committee meeting when one of my colleagues came into the meeting and told me that an hon. member from the province of Ontario was discussing apples. I left the meeting and came here. My riding is not particularly noted for the production of apples, although it is noted for being the greatest agricultural riding in the Dominion of Canada. I am sorry I did not hear what the hon. member from Ontario said, but I shall read Hansard with interest tomorrow to learn what he said about Ontario apples. I can explain even to the member-I have forgotten his title now-who comes from down near London, why we have the great record that we have in British Columbia for our apples. The record of our British Columbia apples is based on our grading and packing. If the rest of Canada, particularly that great old province of Ontario, and to a lesser extent Quebec, would adopt our method of putting out only the best of fruits, and putting them up in the best way possible, they would be able to compete with British Columbia.
I wanted to say one further word on this. I am sorry I had to leave the other committee, but when I am told that something is being said about British Columbia apples I will leave any committee.
I agree with the minister. However, as a private member I can speak more plainly than he can as a cabinet minister. When the people of Great Britain needed our cheese, our butter, our evaporated milk and our fruits, they were delighted to get them to the extent of approximately $3 million as a gift. Since the war has ended they have been quite willing to buy, on a so-called cheaper market, products that have been produced by cheaper labour costs, cheaper production costs, and cheaper costs of all kinds. I think it is time that we talked in plain language to Great Britain. I know all about their foreign exchange control difficulties and the trouble they have in getting money. But after all, if Canada stood behind them in war, as we should have stood behind them, with manpower, financial assistance and assistance in

Supply-Agriculture
every other way, Great Britain should think a little bit more about buying our production, be it agricultural products, fisheries, lumber, or production of any other kind.
I know that the minister cannot say what I can say. I may lose a few votes for saying what I am saying, but I will still have enough to get in. I think my friends over here will agree it is time that we told some of those whom we assisted so much that they owe a little to Canada and to Canadian producers. Coming from British Columbia I do know that our fruit, whether it be apples or other fruits, but particularly small fruits such as strawberries and raspberries of the Fraser valley, are unequalled anywhere in the world.

speechtext: In view of the fact that the minister has not commented on the observations of the hon. member for Durham, are we to assume that any further policy pursued by the dominion government will be acted upon only when a province has taken the initiative in a tree removal program?

I think it is correct to say yes to that. The only continuous tree removal program with which I am familiar in Canada has been carried on by the Nova Scotia government. It was carrying out such a program before the war started. During the war we were asked to take part in it, after we had begun to assist the apple industry in Nova Scotia because they .could not market their apples in Great Britain. Out of that grew a program under which we assisted in paying for apples people could not sell, and taking the trees out so that they would not be there to sell. That was not a tree-pulling campaign, but rather part of a campaign to assist the apple industry of Nova Scotia. At the end of the war the suggestion was made that we
Supply-Agriculture
carry on with that program right across Canada, but we said we would not. A minister of agriculture in one of the provinces came to see me about it, and I stated to him definitely that we were not going to proceed, but that we would expect the province to make a proposal to us under which they would pay at least half of the cost. He smiled and said that we could not be expected to accept that proposal.
That is the policy we are following. We say to the provinces:	If you wish to have a
tree-pulling program, then you must pay a very considerable part of the cost; present your proposal to us and we will consider it. However up to the present we have had no definite proposal other than the Nova Scotia plan except a brief one from Ontario to the effect that they thought the cost ought to be $3 a tree, and asked us if we would consider a program on that basis.

subtopic: APPROVAL OF CONVENTION OF WORLD METEOROLOGICAL ORGANIZATION SIGNED AT WASHINGTON OCTOBER 11, 1947
speechtext: That is, the dominion government was to pay $3 a tree?

subtopic: APPROVAL OF CONVENTION OF WORLD METEOROLOGICAL ORGANIZATION SIGNED AT WASHINGTON OCTOBER 11, 1947
speechtext: We have said that we will not pay the full amount. The position taken at first was for $5 a tree, and we said it would not cost that much to pull a tree or to remove it. Then the next stand was at $4, and we said it would not cost $4. Now the sum is $3, and I presume they mean they will pay half and we will pay half. I do not know exactly what the proposal is.

subtopic: APPROVAL OF CONVENTION OF WORLD METEOROLOGICAL ORGANIZATION SIGNED AT WASHINGTON OCTOBER 11, 1947
speechtext: As the minister has outlined it, the program applies to any province. If a province wishes to institute a tree-removal program it must first put forward its program and a concrete suggestion as to the basis upon which it wishes the dominion to contribute?

speechtext: Yes.

speechtext: Is this program in the minds of the federal authorities primarily an improvement program, so as to bring orchards up to date and enable the growers to have the kind of apples which are more readily marketable, or is it directed primarily to the removal of trees so as to cut down the overall production of apples?

So far as we have taken part in it-and all our activities have been in Nova Scotia-our objective has been to assist in the program they had undertaken and established. I believe they had both things in mind. There were many trees in Nova Scotia producing apples which reached the local market. If they were grown, they were offered for sale. It was better to have improved varieties which could find a market outside Nova Scotia to better advantage. So they were promoting both things, namely, cutting down the number of trees, and

changing the varieties to those which could be sold to better advantage. We helped finance the program during the war. We have not undertaken to do anything about it from then on. The matter is under discussion with the provincial government.

I understand the federal
authorities do not look at this as a program for cutting off production, but rather as an effort to concentrate upon finding markets for better varieties. subtopic: APPROVAL OF CONVENTION OF WORLD METEOROLOGICAL ORGANIZATION SIGNED AT WASHINGTON OCTOBER 11, 1947

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, much has been said about apples, and I think something should be said about the second staff of life, potatoes. I intended to speak on this matter when the first item was before us, but it was passed while I was out of the chamber. At that time the minister referred to this matter, as reported at page 2694 of Hansard of May 19. The king of potato growers and shippers was to have been here today to speak about potatoes-I refer to the hon. member for Victoria-Carleton-but he is unavoidably absent.
Eollowing the minister's remarks there are a few things I should like to place before the committee. Referring to the prices received by the potato growers, mainly those in New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island, the minister said that the average price for the year was 98 cents per hundred pounds, with a price of 99 cents per hundred pounds the year before. The hon. member for Brant then inquired whether that would be the price at the farm, and the minister replied:

I should like to put the record straight in this regard, and say that our people have not been getting the price they should, nor have they been receiving the best consideration from the department. I should like to quote from a report made by the potato industry promotion committee of Prince Edward Island, referred to in the Charlottetown Patriot of May 18 and reading as follows:
It is impossible to accurately estimate the total gross value of the potatoes shipped this year, but it would run at a little better than 50 cents a bushel.

That was the price the potato grower or producer was receiving. The report winds up by saying:
But the province's potato growers were not too happy about the record. It proves once again that the province can produce a bountiful as well as a top-notch crop. But the growers have been taking a financial beating because of the low price.
There has been considerable talk about surplus potatoes, and the suggestion has been

made that the acreage should be reduced. I do not believe there is a surplus; if there is, it is not caused by overproduction so much as by underconsumption. Last year certain agriculture specialists and leading professors in some of the large colleges in the United States endeavoured to And out the eating habits of the people of Canada and the United States, particularly with reference to the consumption of potatoes. It was found that the per capita consumption of potatoes had dropped nearly one bushel per year during the last twenty-five years. As compared with a per capita consumption of three bushels a year, the consumption had been reduced to less than two bushels. With a Canadian population of 13 million people, if the consumption was back to normal the entire Prince Edward Island crop of 13 million bushels could be marketed in this country.
What is the reason for this drop in consumption? It is due largely to dietitians, faddists and others who state that potatoes are fattening. The farmers at one time had the same idea, and they fed large quantities of potatoes to hogs with the idea of fattening them. While they were of some value as food, it was found that there were other things that were much better for fattening purposes. The farmer does not now believe that potatoes are fattening.
Let us go a little further with this question of the use of potatoes as food, and consider the countries that use them most for that purpose. Take, for instance, the people of Ireland, where potatoes were first used as a food and sent out from there to the whole world. What a great food they were! Let us see the effect that potatoes had on the building of a strong and virile manhood. At the age of twenty-one the young men of that country, after living on potatoes three times and sometimes even five times a day-it was their chief food, and should be in every home -left Ireland and brought their virile manhood to New York, Chicago, Philadelphia, Boston, all the large cities of the United States. What are they today? Because of their strong virile manhood they are chiefs of police in ninety-nine towns out of a hundred in the United States. Over eighty per cent of the policemen of the United States were born and bred in Ireland and fed on potatoes day in and day out.
A few years ago flour was more or less sidetracked because some faddist said it was not a really good food, although we know it is a staple of life. The department went to work and advertised the great benefits of flour. They told different stories about what a wonderful food it was, something that we
Supply-Agriculture
all knew. Flour consumption returned to normal. Today what we need is advertising as to the food value of the wonderful potato. Let us break down the ideas of the dietitians and faddists. Let us go a step further and not allow any dietitians employed by the government or the Department of Agriculture to tell people how to cook a potato, because they do not know themselves. The way some of them mash a potato you would not realize what it was. Let the people eating potatoes cook them the way they want to. Let us advertise their food value, and tell the ladies that if they expect a virile race of men they must feed them potatoes. Feed them potatoes, more potatoes, and still more potatoes, because if consumption continues to drop we shall certainly have a surplus. It is not because we are overproducing; it is really because consumption is declining year by year. I hope the minister will see that advertising is carried on to place before the people the benefits of this wonderful food, which is not a luxury but a real food.

Mr. Chairman, following the remarks of the senior member for Queens- I can never satisfy myself which he is-I wish to say that Prince Edward Island produced about 10 million bushels of potatoes in 1949. We shipped 11,000 cars, which is approximately 8,250,000 bushels. If we take another million for domestic purposes and another million for seed, that is approximately 10 million bushels. As to the price, I sold potatoes last fall in our own district through a co-operative company, and the price paid in November for foundation A cobblers was 75 or 80 cents. Later on it dropped as low as 60 cents per bushel. I think one week it went up as high as 92 cents a bushel to the farmer, which is no more than the cost of production.
I kept a record of a sixteen-acre field three years ago as to the cost of fertilizer, seed and labour, and it cost $112 an acre to produce an acre of potatoes. I kept a record of a twenty-acre field last year, and it cost $116 an acre. You can understand that the growing season has a great deal to do with the crop of potatoes. The average production in Prince Edward Island is 200 bushels per acre, and some farmers get as high as 350 and 400 bushels. The revenue from the potato crop accounts for about thirty-five per cent of our annual income.
A great many things could be said about the potato business as I look back over my years of experience since we commenced producing certified seed. The first thing we should have is sufficient storage to look after our crop. Last year I made a survey of storage facilities in Prince Edward Island. There are 102 stations on the Canadian National Railway where potatoes and turnips are assembled and shipped, and at those stations there are frost-proof warehouses with a capacity of 1,600,000 bushels. If you compare that with our production of ten million bushels you will see that we are far short of meeting our storage requirements. At our own station of Douglas we can store forty cars of potatoes. That serves a radius of about ten miles, or four school districts. We have been operating that warehouse on a co-operative basis for the last three years to the satisfaction of everyone, and the farmers have had good returns.

I believe the grant of $100,000 which we receive from the federal government through the Department of Agriculture, as well as the assistance we get from the provincial government, should be used to the fullest extent possible to provide warehouses at the points where they are needed. At Summerside, Charlottetown, Georgetown and Souris we have large warehouses that are used for only about two months in the year for assembling potatoes for water shipment. However, those are not cold storage warehouses where potatoes could be kept for six or eight months. Our potato shipments are not made in one or two months; they extend over eight months of the year.
I believe we should have more storage capacity in order that the marketing of potatoes could be better regulated. We need an orderly marketing system. During the last few years a great deal of cutthroat competition has been going on among the dealers, large and small. I keep track of the markets in the larger cities, such as Toronto, Ottawa and Montreal, as well as western Canada. Many times I have been in those centres and have seen wires received in the morning quoting potato prices varying from ten to twenty-five cents per bag. You can see how confusing that is to the buyers. If we had an orderly marketing system we would be able to do away with this competition, as well as with the consignment of potatoes to over-depressed markets.
When I was in Toronto this year potatoes were selling for as little as $1.18 for a 75-pound bag, delivered. When you take away the price of the bag and the cost of freight, the dealer back in Prince Edward Island has left only about 60 cents, and you can see what the grower gets after the dealer takes his small commission. In the last eighteen months the freight rate has increased by 16 cents per hundred. For the last ten years the rate to Toronto was 39 cents. Now it is 55 cents. Someone says that can be passed on to the consumer, but I do not know whether that can be done. This high freight rate has made a great difference in the returns to our potato growers.
Over the last twenty-five years our producers have learned all about growing and grading potatoes. As I see it, the only problem now is marketing. As I said a moment ago, if we had an orderly marketing system I believe many of our difficulties would be overcome. We have the finest potato inspection service in existence, both with respect to table stock and seed potatoes. This service has been developed under two able men. One is Mr. Peppin, of the seed department, who I am sorry to say is leaving the service next year because of his age, and

who has done a wonderful job over the last thirty years. The other is Mr. Chester E. Shaw, the chief table stock inspector, who is also retiring in about another year. I am sure everyone who knows what he has done for the potato growers of Prince Edward Island will have a word of praise for him.
I could go on for an hour; in fact I could write a book on the potato business, having been connected with it since 1921. I have seen many ups and downs. Many people have gone broke in the potato business, though for the last few years the growers, and the dealers especially, have done very well. To solve our problems, however, we should have more and better storage facilities, and the growers themsplves should make some suggestions to the government that would bring about a system of orderly marketing. I have been speaking to many people in Ottawa and Toronto who say they would be quite willing to pay a decent price for potatoes, which this year were much cheaper than other foods on the market. I believe we must blame ourselves for this system of marketing, which can be corrected by those in the industry. I do not think we can blame the federal government.
Last year many representations were made to the Department of Agriculture with respect to a floor price. Well, if you start paying floor prices you never get to the end of it. I do not believe in a floor price unless you have control of the acreage, because if a farmer is making the cost of production he will keep on growing potatoes. In Prince Edward Island and the maritimes we are like the people In western Canada; we are great "next year" people; we always hope that next year will be a killer and we will make a lot of money.
I do not believe it is necessary for me to say anything more. The senior member for Queens understands the situation in our little province as well as I do, and I am sure both he and I will be glad to do everything possible to help the potato growers. I should like to give just one quotation that I read in the newspapers, credited to the New Brunswick minister of agriculture, who said: "We are still carrying on the same old antiquated marketing system we had fifty years ago." I thought that was the truest thing I had heard in many a day, and I heartily agree. It is up to ourselves to improve the situation and help our people who, after spending their time and money, after getting up at three o'clock in the morning to spray potatoes, after wearing out machinery, at the end of the year find they have scarcely enough money to pay the fertilizer bill.

Mr. Chairman, as I recall the remarks which were made by the member for Northumberland and the member for Durham, they were calling attention to the fact that financial assistance had been given to the apple growers in other parts of Canada but not the Ontario growers. That is true, of course. On a previous occasion I believe I indicated that other assistance had been given the Ontario apple growers during the war period. It was indirect assistance, because the apples from British Columbia and Nova Scotia were ruled out of the central Canada market until permits were issued for the marketing of them. This left the best market in Canada open to Ontario and Quebec apples.
Later the action taken was not quite so drastic, but we did have an understanding with the Nova Scotia and British Columbia apple producers that they would not put their apples into that market until a certain time of the year. This understanding was religiously carried out until last year. The result has been that the apple growers in Ontario, and I think they will agree with me, received the best returns they ever had for their apples during that ten-year period. Last year again there was considerable care taken with the marketing. When the season opened we told both British Columbia and Nova Scotia that we were not making an agreement in advance this year covering the marketing of the crop. We were prepared to consider what had happened at the end of the marketing season, and deal with the situation on the basis of actual results.
When the end of the season arrived, we checked the returns which the Ontario growers received as well as the returns received by the growers in the other two provinces. Even after assistance had been given to British Columbia and Nova Scotia, the returns obtained for apples in Ontario were considerably higher than in those areas. There is no reason, therefore, why the government should assist Ontario in obtaining a higher level than that which has been attained, unless we are prepared to raise the returns received in British Columbia and Nova Scotia to a higher point. The Ontario returns are still higher than the returns in either of the other places.
As I understand the question, it related to whether assistance is to be given in the future. The only legislation under which
assistance could be provided in connection with price levels is the Agricultural Prices Support Act. The apple producer has a right to expect consideration under that act, the same as any other agricultural producer in Canada. The question would be considered on its merits when the application is made. No undertaking can be given in advance. It is a matter that will be dealt with on its merits when the time arrives.

I wish to refer to a statement made by the minister last night, and repeated in other words this morning, which it seems to me does call for clarification. That is particularly so in view of the fact that here in Ottawa at the present time are representatives of the press from every part of the commonwealth.
Throughout the whole of Canada today the Canadian Press has carried a dispatch based upon a statement made by the minister last night. I quote now from the Canadian Press dispatch:
Agriculture Minister Gardiner indicated tonight he thinks it is time Canada started to talk tough to Britain in trading matters.
It is time, he told the commons, that Canada stopped talking nicely to some people in Britain when she tried to obtain British markets for Canadian food products. It was time for "more direct" talk by Canada.
That statement by the minister may well be a statement that should have been made; but the minister has said either too much or too little. This is the kind of statement which very naturally and very properly will receive considerable attention in the United Kingdom. If this statement was intended to be taken seriously, as I think it was, then it is important that the minister should go further and say exactly what he does mean; and he should indicate whom it is he is talking about.
There is not, I suggest, any doubt, in the minds of members of this House of Commons that the people of Britain have every desire to trade with the people of Canada. I do not think there is any thought in the minds of members of the house that the people of Great Britain would not willingly wish to have arrangements made which would make available to them the products of this country.
The statement is made that there are some people who should be spoken to in a much firmer way than they have been spoken to before. I think we should know whether those are members of the present government of Great Britain, and I do not know why we should be left to guess as to who they are. After all, the way this matter stands today, a very important statement has been made affecting the relationship of two countries in

trade matters, affecting the relationship of two governments, and I think it should be specific.
I think there is an added reason why it should be specific, and that is that there is also carried in today's press a very important statement from Great Britain. The Canadian Press also carries a report of its correspondent newspapers today which reports on a decision by the party which forms the present government in the United Kingdom. This has some possible relationship to the statement that was made, and cannot therefore be ignored. If it has no relationship, then I think we should know it.
In an announced decision of the party from which the government of the United Kingdom is formed it is stated that they last night reached a decision based upon a statement prepared by the Hon. Hugh Dalton, who is a member of the cabinet of the United Kingdom, and was presenting this statement in his capacity as a member of the executive of the party to which he belongs. In this particular case they are explaining the reasons why they reached the decision not to enter into a plan for the pooling of resources of a certain type throughout Europe, with which it had been suggested that they might be associated. And in that statement that was given in support of their decision not to agree to join in that plan, the party which forms the present government of the United Kingdom is responsible for this statement, among others:
Socialists would of course welcome a European economic union which was based on international planning for full employment, social justice and stability. But international planning can only operate on the basis of national planning. And many European governments have not yet shown either the will or the ability to plan their own economies.
That paragraph in the statement issued last night has already been interpreted by the responsible press in Great Britain and elsewhere as a declaration that the government of Great Britain is being guided in certain of its actions by its willingness or otherwise to deal with those countries which are accepting certain doctrines of which they approve.
In view of the fact that this statement appears at the very same time as the statement >by the Minister of Agriculture to the effect that there are certain people who should be spoken to frankly, then I think his statement should go further and indicate whether it has any relationship whatever to the insistence upon the acceptance of certain types of sale and purchase related to political doctrines, or whether there are other reasons. Also he should tell us who the people are
Supply-Agriculture
to whom we should direct these franker points of view, which might have some practical results.
May I say as one member of the House of Commons that in connection with any dealing with Great Britain or any other country' my first concern is certainly the advantage of the people of Canada. If any steps are being taken to our disadvantage, then I think we should have full information, and I think also that all of us should join in a perfectly frank expression of our opinion.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, in reference to the words used last night, I do not think it is necessary to take them from the press, because they are in Hansard-and they are much more correct in Hansard than they are in the press. They are not so different, except as to the first term that was used. These are the words:
I think it is about time we stopped talking nicely to some people over in Britain. That does not apply to very many people, just one or two; but until they are spoken to directly I do not think we should look for very much success in the marketing of some of those products in that country.
At that time we were discussing the item relating to apples. I still maintain that that is correct. Coming down to the suggestion that it might result from the attitude of some political party, I would answer that by saying this, that the plan under which we operated from 1940 until 1948 was a plan which was set up under the Churchill government, with Lord Woolton as minister of food. The system of having the government purchase food coming from outside of Britain as well as food produced in Britain was set up by the Churchill government. It was continued in much the same form at least until 1948, and probably is still continued in Great Britain in relation to most countries.
Under that plan it did not make any difference which government was in power, whether it was a Conservative government, a coalition government or the present socialist government. The general plan was to take all the food they could get from Canada-that was their attitude-and our attitude was to supply all the food we could. When we met together to discuss the question it was merely a matter from their point of view of how much we could give them, and from our point of view it was a question of what they were able to pay for it. We entered into an agreement and we then went out to our farmers and asked them to produce enough so that we could at least provide the quantity which they desired to have. That was the general trend of it.
But as I said last session, when we got along to 1947 it was intimated that that was not their general desire, that what they

Supply-Agriculture
would like us to do was to cut out everything but wheat. We suggested that that was going to be most difficult. We were prepared to co-operate as far as it was possible to co-operate in getting our sales made elsewhere or in our own markets at home in order to consume the food we were producing and we did co-operate in every possible way in getting that done. We have been co-operating in every possible way down to the present in getting that done.
Up until now we have been able to market our farm products. We have not very much complaint about the prices of farm products, which are just as good or a little better in this country than they are in most places, with one or two exceptions. For that reason we are not complaining about what the farmer is getting for the products he has to sell. He is doing as well now as he has ever done in selling his products.
I am sure many people, either in this house or outside, have the feeling, and it certainly is true among farmers throughout the country, that we are not always going to be able to eat all that we produce or even as great a percentage of what we produce as we are able to eat at the present time. Some people think that the natural place to sell any surplus we have is in the United States; some think that the natural place to sell it is in Great Britain; but in my opinion the natural place to sell it is in both places to the extent that it can be sold.
I think that when our friends who depended upon us so greatly during wartime for food are going to take the position, "Well, we would like to get food anywhere but in Canada," we should not even attempt to say anything different from what I have said either in this house or outside this house, with regard to their attitude. I do not care whether that attitude is the attitude of the government or of the opposition. The last time I was in Great Britain they invited me to sit in the gallery and there was a debate on food put on. I listened to it and afterward I told them what my impression was. I was told that they thought that that would be my impression when they asked me to sit in the gallery. My impression was there were there many people who were concerned, and properly so, about getting all the food they possibly could produced within Britain. That has been the long-term Conservative policy in Great Britain, and it is still the policy in that country. There was not much difference between the two sides of the house on that particular question. Their first desire, like ours, is to produce in Great Britain all they can. Then their second desire is to have

it sold at as good a price as possible in their own market, and they subsidize the sale of it before it goes to their people.
We are a little differently situated. I personally think most hon. members-and I am quite certain the leader of the opposition thinks likewise-should pride themselves on the fact that we belong to the British commonwealth. For many years we prided ourselves on the fact that we belonged to the British empire, but in more recent years we have called it the commonwealth of nations. I may be wrong, and if I am I am quite prepared to be considered wrong, but I do not think there has ever been a better organization set up in the world, and I include the United Nations, to promote peace throughout the world than the British commonwealth of nations.
I think it most important that our relationships with the centre of the empire should be of the most cordial kind and I believe the manner in which they can remain on that basis as between a considerable part of the population of this country and of Great Britain is for them to take our food in the same free way during peacetime as they did during wartime. That is what I meant by saying that we should speak to them bluntly.
I do not think there is any dollar-sterling question in the world or any dollar-sterling problem as between Canada and Great Britain that is more important than the maintenance of good relationships between those two areas. That is all I meant by what I said, and that is what I still mean and that is what I am still prepared to say, either in the house or outside. I think it is the duty of Canada to produce all the food for Great Britain she can, and I think it is equally the duty of Great Britain to buy all the food she can from us rather than to go elsewhere for it. If they do that and if we keep up our production I think we are both going to be better off even if it does take some dollars that they otherwise would pile up.
It would have required only $30 million last year for Great Britain to have satisfied all the demands of agriculture in this country as to the sale of food. If the $30 million had been proffered, under the plan of cooperation in solving their problems as well as our own, I venture to say that they would not have had to use half of it. Our people would have been perfectly satisfied that they were being treated properly, and their people would have been perfectly satisfied that they were getting all the surplus food there was from this country. With a question as simple as that I do not think we should be carrying on controversy and discussion as to whether Great Britain should take our apples or

whether she should take the little bit of pork we have. When I said a little bit last year some people were inclined to scoff, but it has turned out to be even smaller than I thought it would be. I thought we were going to have 60 million pounds by this time and we have only 12 million pounds. When this problem is such a small one, I think all this talk about its being caused by the fact that there is some dollar-sterling problem just is not the case at all.
If we could get that into the minds of one or two people probably we could settle the question so far as Great Britain and Canada are concerned. We are not going to settle the dollar-sterling question so far as the world is concerned. But I repeat, I think it is important that we produce as much food as we can for Great Britain, and I think it is important that Great Britain should take as much of it as she can take, important from the point of view not only of ourselves and herself but of the whole world over a period.

As may be recalled, we have introduced a number of resolutions whjch had as their purpose the presentation of that very point of view. When the Minister of Agriculture says that he hopes there will be those who will understand that there is no dollar-sterling problem nearly as important as arranging for this sale, I hope he will convince the Minister of Finance of that very fact, because in answer to our argument along that line we have been told by the Minister of Finance that this is an insurmountable barrier. The minister has not yet answered the question I put to him. Frankness is just as desirable in one's own family as outside, and perhaps more so, and if frankness is desirable in this case then at least put us all in the position where we can join in being equally frank, and tell us who these one or two people are who need to be spoken to. We know it is not the people of Great Britain generally, and I think it is desirable that there be complete frankness.
I certainly concur in all the minister has said about the importance of the trade between Great Britain and Canada. Since this subject has been brought up by the minister, I would go further and say that Canadians cannot look without some measure of concern at the published statements that some of the food products we have been supplying are now being bought from countries behind the iron curtain. There may be explanations for that, but I think we would be less than frank if we did not say quite clearly to these friends

who are so close to us that the purchase of things which we produce from countries against which we are arrayed in so many ways can only create uncertainties at this time. Whether we call it an empire or a commonwealth, the main thing is that it is the greatest partnership of free nations that the world has ever known. If frankness will help to remove any ground of misunderstanding, then I think all hon. members will welcome the opportunity to be quite as frank as the minister, but I think it would help if we knew where to direct our remarks.

Item 29 includes an amount not to exceed $6,000 which is to be used for temporary appointments that may be required, notwithstanding anything contained in the Civil Service Act. I have not gone back to the year one, but I have gone back a few years, and I find that this item has been in the estimates at least since 1945. The total amount of the vote has been increased from $25,000 five years ago to $100,000 now. I should like to point out that the portion of the vote about which I am talking, namely, the item for appointments notwithstanding the provisions of the Civil Service Act, has been reduced. The amount available for such appointment or appointments used to be $15,000, and now it is only $6,000. I wonder whether the minister is aware of the fact that this is one of the items about which the Auditor General has commented in his memorandum to the Senate and to the public accounts committee of the House of Commons this year. His comment centres around the fact that this is the kind of item in the estimates that has legislative effect without parliament having gone through the normal procedure to provide for such legislation.
The Civil Service Act makes provision as to how people are to be appointed, but in this case apparently some one or more persons are being appointed to allegedly temporary positions notwithstanding the provisions of the Civil Service Act. In all fairness I should point out that the Auditor General recognizes the convenience of this procedure for temporary appointments. However, he deprecates the practice of repeating it year after year. As a matter of fact there are some twenty or thirty items throughout the estimates to which the Auditor General calls attention under this general heading. This happens to be the only one that he points out in the estimates of the Department of Agriculture, so far as the practice of legislating by items in the estimates is concerned. I would like the minister to tell me how many persons are covered by this $6,000 portion of the item now before us. If it is only one person I should like to know how long that person has held the position. Perhaps I can get that information and then ask .my next question.

My information is that only one position is set up under this amount at the present time, and that position is on the staff of Mr. Robertson over in London. It was occupied for some time by a lady, whose name I do not have at the moment, and the position has to do with the publicizing our marketing possibilities in Great Britain. This item, which has been increased from $25,000 to $100,000, is the general marketing item in the department. Up to last year we did not use it to the extent we are using it now. The largest item being spent under it is the $50,000 we are using to advertise butter and dairy products. Another item will be the $12,000 we are going to utilize to advertise honey and other products. We set up the amount for the purpose of having money available that can be utilized for that kind of work when it is necessary; and those who might be appointed to such positions, either in this country or in Britain, would be people associated with the promotion of those sales. Judging from the position, the person in Britain occupying it would be engaged in keeping records more than anything else; but this whole amount would not be paid to that individual. It is an amount we could use, if we desired, to put a person on the road in connection with the advertising of butter, for example, to offset the advertising of oleomargarine. We might put a person on the road for that purpose for a. time without having to wait for an appointment under the civil service commission.
If I might give an example, last March we discovered that all over Canada there were stores that had no butter at all. They were selling margarine only. I assume the reason was that they were not fully informed as to what the government was prepared to do after April 1, when there was to be a reduction in the price of butter. They were making absolutely sure they would not have to take the five cent drop, so they had no butter at all in stock at the end of the month. That would have something to do with the size of the surplus we had to carry at the end of the year; and if it were desired to do so, under this item we could send persons out on the road for two or three weeks without waiting for appointments by the civil service commission, in order to correct such a situation.

On the other hand a great number of people have been agitating that we tell the farmers of this country how to produce a lot more milk with less effort, and more butter with less effort. These people are advocating the spending of a great deal of money to tell the farmers how to sell it. I want to say that more money should be spent in telling the farmers how to co-operate amongst themselves in putting forth their own publicity. They should be told how to organize properly so that the people will know the value of their products and will buy them.
I have advocated this in my own riding. I have told the farmers to get together and tell the world what they produce. I have suggested that they call meetings to see if they can get some constructive ideas, and that they should bring in marketing experts. I am sorry to say there has been little response to that suggestion. This has to be a two-way street. If the government is going to spend a lot of money helping the farmers-and I am sure the rest of the farmers in Canada are no different from those in my constituency-then those farmers have to pull their weight. They should try to see that taxes are cut, and that the price of food is lowered so that people can buy it. Nobody can buy their products today. There should be more people advocating more effort on the part of my friends the farmers. I have said this directly to the farmers. We can give these farmers too much. Soon they will be spoon-fed and cradle-rocked. They have to go along with the government, and try to reduce taxes and produce better results. They have to sell a greater quantity with more effort contributed by the farmer.
Now some members who represent purely rural constituencies are going to glower at me and say, "He should not talk that way; he will lose votes." I do not think I will lose many votes. I shall have the votes of better farmers and richer farmers if they will listen to reason, and get together to market their products. The finest apples in the world are produced in my county. There is no argument about that, because they won all the prizes. I have suggested to those men that they sell the apples in smaller cartons, so that a woman would not be asked to go out of a chain store with 105 apples under her arm; something she could not possibly do. At the

same time, she would have liked to buy ten apples. A woman living in an apartment cannot possibly consume 105 apples before they go bad. There is no place to keep them. Yet these men have gone on for years trying to force down the throats of the people large hampers of apples. Their attitude is: take them or leave them. For years I have advocated that the apples be packed in small cartons containing ten or eleven apples, so that a person could put it in a basket and take it home. The apples could be kept in the cold storage plants until needed, and packed in these small cartons.
Last fall the farmers were whining about whether they would get rid of their apples. I tasted Northern Spies from the cold storage plant at Thornbury not more than three weeks ago, and they were as fresh as when they were picked off the trees last fall. As a matter of fact they were improved. Last fall these men were trying to market them in barrels or hampers. A woman could not possibly take home a barrel or hamper and keep the apples without the proper refrigeration.
I do hope the government will do something to tell the farmers of Canada how they can start helping themselves to some extent. A large number of them do work together and sell their products intelligently, but there are still a large number who will not get on the bandwagon. They want to be outlaws; they want to cry and whine. They do cry and whine. May I suggest to the minister that, on the cheapest, unglossed paper, he tell the farmers in no uncertain terms about the lack of common-sense business methods used by the farmers in their selling. I hope that will be done. Then less of the general taxpayers' money will be spent in publishing "Five Ways to Cook Apples". I saw one pamphlet with that title, published by the department. If the people of Canada have to be told how to cook apples, I think they had better go without them.

speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I do not think this is the place for hon. members to begin quarrelling about the farmers and saying things against them. I know enough about farmers and the job they are doing to know that they should not be criticized by any member. If the hon. member thinks the position of the farmer is better than the position of member of parliament, he ought to try it. He will soon find out. The farmers have no complaint against this federal government; they have only thanks for the best Minister of Agriculture we have ever had. Every dollar that has been spent to help the farmer of this country is money well spent. My riding is a little more urban than rural. I have to speak on behalf of both sections. We have not too much production. If our farmers lose money on their production we have to help them out. If they are losing money on the production of butter it is because of margarine. The labouring people of this country are sufficiently well off to eat good food. They should eat butter, subsidized by the government if it is necessary to sell it at a cheaper price. People should not eat that old margarine which is going to cost millions and millions of dollars because of its effect on butter production. subtopic: APPROVAL OF CONVENTION OF WORLD METEOROLOGICAL ORGANIZATION SIGNED AT WASHINGTON OCTOBER 11, 1947
speechtext: I wonder if this committee knows that of all the money collected in Canada by taxation the farmer gets two cents out of every dollar. speechtext: I notice that this item is for freight assistance on western feed grains. In 1949-50 the amount was $17 million. This year it is $5 million, a difference of $12 million. As the minister knows, we are greatly interested in eastern Canada in assistance on feed grains, especially in the maritimes, because to a great extent the success of our farmers depends on getting cheap feed for their hogs and their cattle. speechtext:
No, it does not mean either. The amount of $5 million is the amount necessary to cover the cost down to the 31st day of July, because this is the way it has always been voted. The original vote has always been an amount to carry it through the crop year we are in. The year spoken of is the grain year which begins on August 1 and ends on July 31. I have proposed that there be $13 million in the supplementary estimates to cover the remainder. It has come down previously in two votes, one for the main vote and one for the supple-mentaries. That question is another which was discussed at the same time as the

previous question that I brought up with regard to hogs. It has been decided just today so that there was no possibility of making the announcement earlier.
This is not a vote which necessarily goes on from year to year. It is voted annually, and has been ever since the beginning. The origin of the vote is that the maritime provinces were very anxious to have part of their freight removed because of the high cost of getting feed from western Canada to the extreme east of the country. There was an agitation for that before the war started at all. We were considering the possibility of doing it in the maritimes. I think it was early in 1941 we decided to pay a quarter of the freight. Very shortly after that we brought in price control, in the latter part of 1941, and then we changed over from paying a portion of the freight to the paying of what we expected would be nearly all the freight in all of the eastern provinces and in the province of British Columbia. The freight is paid from Fort William to a location in the eastern part of Canada, and from Calgary and Edmonton into the province of British Columbia. This vote has been, as I say, renewed from year to year. We said a year ago, and I think the year before that, that it was the intention to have the whole question of discrimination in freight rates studied by a commission and a report made upon it. We have always called attention to the fact that this policy will probably be given fuller consideration when that report comes in. It will then be determined whether we are going on with the policy or whether we are going to have some other plan of equalization which will bring results. In any case what I wish to emphasize is that this is just a year to year vote. It is made in two amounts because we continue it until the end of the crop year. We have enough money to take us from April 1 to the end of the crop year, in the regular estimates, and then if we determine to go on for the complete crop year we put an amount in the supplementary estimates. That amount will be in the supple-mentaries this year.
