speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, in the national interest I believe that, on an item of such magnitude as the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act, any member who is in a position to offer any suggestions whereby some of this expenditure may be eliminated in the future in connection with this item as well as the Prairie Farm Assistance Act should endeavour to make whatever contribution he can. I should like to state briefly what I have to say because I do not wish to prolong the session. From my observations most of the time has been taken by the opposition, so I would ask them please to bear with me for a few minutes in order that I may put the conditions at home before this house.
I have been existing, and I repeat "existing", in the constituency of Maple Creek for thirty-three years. Many of those years have been spent in scanning the horizon in the hope that it would rain. Most of the people living in that area have been doing the same thing. As a consequence it is my duty, as the member representing that district, to say a word in connection with the rehabilitation of those people. It is not my intention to repeat what the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act has already accomplished in connection with the building of thousands of small irrigation projects and small dams in that area. I know they number in the thousands. Community pastures number nearly a hundred. Then there has been the moving of the people and the regrassing that has taken place in that area under this item. I believe that if a member can suggest anything that might possibly hasten the process of rehabilitation of these people he should certainly do so.
The Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act was established to correct in the future the mistakes of the past. This act, or its counterpart, has been in existence in some part of the world ever since the beginning of time, because it is part and parcel of agriculture.

It is only history that tells us whether agriculture is feasible in any area. If after the people are settled in an area for a period of time it is determined the soil is. not suitable for agriculture, then the rehabilitation of those people has to take place. We have heard much about the floods in Winnipeg and the other disasters that have happened in this country. I do not know of a greater disaster that can happen to people than that those people should live in an area for a lifetime and not be in a position to earn their living. They then find that they will have to leave that area in which they have laboured so long and begin life anew in some other area; that is what the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act proposed to do and has done for many people in that area. If it is to be done, the sooner the better.
For many days we have been talking about areas in the central part of Canada that have had too much water. As everyone knows, the area of which I am speaking has too little water. The problem this presents is too great for the individual, so society, through this government, comes to the assistance of the individual. Mr. Chairman, we wish to hasten the process of alleviating suffering in that area. Again this spring in the municipalities surrounding my home over
510,000	bushels of seed grain had to be supplied to these people. Vegetables were shipped into some parts of the area during last fall to enable the people to live through the winter. This means that under the P.F.A.A. the people are not receiving sufficient to keep themselves for a year. The cost of living today is entirely different from the cost ten years ago, yet today the maximum amount obtainable under the P.F.A.A. is exactly the same as it was ten years ago. I have heard it stated that some of the farmers in the drought area are living and farming for P.F.A.A. benefits. I would make it clear that there is not one farmer in that area doing that because to operate the average farm it costs between $2,500 and $4,000. The maximum amount any farmer can receive in one year under the Prairie Farm Assistance Act is $500. One can imagine, therefore, what would happen in that area over a period of years, if anyone was farming for P.F.A.A. alone.
In the area of which I am speaking there is a rainfall of from twelve to fourteen inches. The situation is entirely different from what it is in other areas such as Ottawa, where I understand the rainfall is between twenty and thirty inches. Under the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act, through the co-operation of the federal and provincial governments, methods have been devised whereby the people may

be able to live there in the future and make their living. I am saying that because I wish to leave this committee with the idea that the money which has been spent thus far in dealing with the matter has been well spent. I wish to tell the committee that the larger the appropriations are under the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act, the smaller the appropriations are going to be under the Prairie Farm Assistance Act in the future. It is that ideal towards which we are striving. We want to enable every farming community throughout the length and breadth of Canada to stand on its own feet. Then, crop failure assistance will not be necessary. The farmers living in those areas, wherever they may be, would be able to take their place along with the rest of the people of Canada, and make their contribution to the country as a whole.
In these areas we have the triple S system of farming, that is the summer-fallow system. It means that we have to allow the land to rest one year to accumulate moisture so that we will have enough moisture for the next year. We have to have two years' moisture to grow one crop. Under this system we have to summer-fallow the grass also. We have not been doing so well at that, and last year the grass did not come up on my farm at all. As I say, we have to summer-fallow the grass so that our stock will have something to fall back upon. We have to summer-fallow the water because we have about 6,000 small irrigation projects. I am not speaking of the larger ones because even at the best, with all the larger irrigation projects one hears about, only about one-tenth of the land can be irrigated. What are we going to do with the rest of it? The altitude of my farm is about 2,880 feet, and that is about 900 feet higher than the average land in Saskatchewan. How is water going to be forced up to that land? As I have said, in spite of these large irrigation projects, only about one-tenth of the land can be irrigated.
We are interested in knowing how these farmers can assist themselves in places where the land cannot be irrigated, and cannot be looked after by means of this summer-fallow system. I suppose it will have to be done by impounding the water on a small scale on the various farms. This will mean that if one dam is built and that fills with water, you will have to build another one because there will be some years when the first dam will not be filled with water. You have to summer-fallow water as well as everything else. On that basis it will mean larger farms. We have heard in this committee that it takes from forty to fifty acres of pasture to sustain an animal, and that is possibly true. As the Minister of Agriculture pointed out, sometimes 55946-226J
Supply-Agriculture
cattle can subsist on a smaller number of acres in other areas so our farms will have to be larger to make them self-sustaining. In that case I suppose some of our people will want to move to other areas.
I do not want to be too long, Mr. Chairman, but I do want to say that in my opinion not enough attention has been paid to grasses. Any member of this house who has had anything to do with agriculture can identify wheat, oats, barley, rye and flax plants if I hold them in my hand, but how many could identify the plants of five of the native grasses? I do not suppose anyone could name those five native grasses; at least I know I could not. This fact was brought forcibly to my attention by one of the scientific men at the Swift Current experimental farm whose name was Heinricks, and it has stayed with me because I believe it is more important in the general agricultural picture throughout the world than we realize. We should realize that it is grass that keeps the earth in place. I think more money could properly be expended in a scientific inquiry to determine what improvements could be made in these various grasses. Grass is the only possible crop in so many of our areas.
I would like to point out, Mr. Chairman, that some of the townships in the western part of Saskatchewan, the southwestern part, and in Alberta have been receiving crop failure payments for ten years. If the past is any indication of the future it would appear to me, and to many others, that possibly for the next ten years these same lands will receive the same amount of money in crop failure payments. Therefore if these 44 townships over the past ten years have received $5,000 it would mean that this government, or the government of Canada, if history repeats itself, will have to pay the same lands that same amount of money, namely, $5,000 in the next ten-year period, or in the next fifteen or twenty-year period, whatever the case may be. It is well known that history always repeats itself.
I understand that there are thousands of applications from people who want to move to other areas where they may make a living and absolve themselves from this unhappiness that has been going on there for years. The land where these people are to move on is not available at the present time. We hear members of parliament and others suggest that there are hundreds of acres here, there and elsewhere that they would like people to move to. But you cannot take people who are fifty and sixty years old and who have worked all their life and put them in a bush area that is not cleared, and where they have to start all over again to make

Supply-Agriculture
their living. You have to provide some other means tor them. Therefore I was wondering whether we could not change the basis of movement and bring in a voluntary movement. By that I mean instead of the government undertaking to move them it could be done in this way. Let us assume that in the 44 townships I have mentioned we are going to have to pay $5,000 a farm for the next ten years. Why not make the $5,000 available to those people in one lump sum? If that were done I am sure they would find a place to move to and make themselves self-sustaining on their own, without any additional assistance. They would find a place somewhere in this country of ours to which they could go, and not have to go where the government would have to place them. If that system were inaugurated they could go voluntarily.
The reason these people are not moving is that they have not enough money to move. It takes money to move. They have to depend on the government assisting them. If this were made voluntary they could move on their own and the government would not be spending any more money. I am sure it would relieve the situation to some extent, a situation which is going to be aggravated if there is another extensive crop failure this year, if means were provided whereby they could move voluntarily and make their own living.

If something could be done to keep the water where it is originally impounded in the spring it would be a great help to those people who stay there, and they would be able at least to provide water for their gardens and their small irrigation projects, and that would at least make it possible for them to stay there.
This is all the time that I would dare ask the chairman to give me at this time. We base it all on the assumption that in the future in that area of ours we are going to develop a system through P.F.R.A. whereby the people can make their own living and be happy along with the other people in Canada.
That means the summer-fallow system that I have outlined, the scientific sealing of dams, the economic unit of farms and ranches, contour farming, which is being practised in this country at the present time, and all in all to bring about a system and a policy whereby these people, working along with the other people of Canada, will make their contribution, which is the effort and the desire of all of us.

What happens is pretty much what is happening in connection with the project to which the hon. member has referred. The engineers have been there since the spring. That is the beginning of any construction. As has been said, first an application is made. Then we send men there to make a survey of the possibilities. They go and look the country over. They may or they may not be engineers. Then they will decide whether the plan is feasible. Once we decide a project should be proceeded with we call in the engineers so that they may go over it, check the whole area and give us estimates as to costs and other related matters. Then, as a rule, we have soil surveys to indicate whether water can be put on it successfully. We ascertain the necessity for drainage, and all that kind of thing. We do not say definitely that we will proceed with any project until all that work is done. If that work reveals that it is a project which will be helpful to the community, we then proceed with it.

speechtext:
I want to say how pleased we are in our part of the country to have the P.F.R.A. So far as the land is concerned it is good soil and will hold water. In past years there was plenty of surface water but as the years have gone by we have had to go farther and farther north to find such a condition. The northern part of my constituency used to be well supplied with all kinds of water but the water level has dropped, and today the people have to dig dugouts. These small projects are dugouts 65 feet wide, 175 feet long and 12 feet deep involving the removal of 2,500 square yards of earth in their construction. The water there is sufficient to cover an acre to a depth of a foot. The water is gathered in the dugout mostly in the spring of the year, is stored there, and generally there is enough rain to keep it up to that level. It provides water all summer and all winter for the people, and enables them to keep stock in that part of the country that otherwise would not be there. They would have to get rid of them.
It is not a grain growing country. It is bush, but for some reason the water level has gone down over a period of years. In one part of my constituency they are drawing water a distance of twenty miles, and they are not in a P.F.R.A. area. I should like to ask the minister to try to extend the area covered by P.F.R.A. farther north so that these people can receive some assistance and retain their stock. The assistance is only small but it helps the farmer to co-operate with the man who has the heavy machinery necessary to dig the dugout.
The people in the area are on small homesteads of a quarter or half section. A lot of the land has bush on it. Some of the people only have 25, 30, 40 or 50 acres of land broken, but they have to have water for their stock. I would ask the minister to do something about moving the line farther north so that these people can receive the benefits of the P.F.R.A. I am not going to take any more time. I have a 16-page speech that I had intended to deliver on the subject of P.F.R.A. In our municipality we have 600 dugouts, and I will not rest until we have one on every quarter-section in the municipality. If there is any salvation for such a community it is water. When you have water you have a certain amount of protection from insects. Birds will remain in the region if you have bush and water, but if

Supply-Agriculture
you have no water the birds will leave. They attack all kinds of insects that destroy crops. If you do not have birds where you grow grain sooner or later you will suffer from the attacks of insects, because that is what happens in the long run. Over a period of years it has happened all over the world. Where you do not have birds you have poor crops because insects ultimately come along and devour them.
I want to say a few words about crop conditions in that part of the country, conditions that may come some day to the people of eastern Canada. I heard one man say today that they needed rain in this part of the country, and if they did not get rain they would soon be in a pretty bad condition. That is often the case in western Canada, and it was for that reason that P.F.R.A. was started. I should like to say that instead of the item being $3 million it should be $30 million. It should be available to help all the people of Canada, and the sooner we start to develop Canada in that spirit the better it will be for us. The farmer is the foundation of the country. He is the one who provides food for the people of Canada to eat, and the amount that the people of Canada spend on him is very small.

speechtext:
I should like to say a word about prairie farm rehabilitation. Unlike the hon. member for Maple Creek I am not so much interested in rehabilitation as I am in the small projects mentioned by the hon. member for Mackenzie. When the P.F.R.A. legislation was introduced in the west in the first place, and in Saskatchewan, in which I am particularly interested, it was brought in to cover what was then the dry part of the prairie provinces. As the hon. member for Mackenzie has said, the dry area has extended somewhat farther north. In the constituency I represent it now affects the southern part of my riding to a depth of 50 to 100 miles. The top 250 to 300 miles has a good supply of water but the bottom 50 to 100 miles is getting fairly short. The water table in the latter region has dropped some 20 or 25 feet, and it is beginning to affect the people who are raising livestock. We are not in the same position as people farther south in Saskatchewan who raise grain entirely, and who are in a serious plight if they do not have a crop. As long as we have some feed and water, there is always plenty of livestock to keep the people in good shape financially.
The point I want to make is that the money spent on these small dams is not something that is poured into the west and never comes back to the east. So long as these people are able to raise livestock they are always in
[Mr. Ferried
good financial condition and are able to buy the products of the east. I want to bring this point to the attention of hon. members because sometimes it appears from all these votes for P.F.R.A. that we are pouring money into a pail with a hole in the bottom. So far as small projects are concerned in an area of that kind, that is definitely not the case because livestock constitute the insurance policy of these people. The expenditure on these small dams only amounts to about $150 each, but when each farmer has water he knows that his stock are going to be taken care of, and that he will not have to get rid of them on short notice.
Practically every municipality in an area of some 50 to 100 miles in the southern portion of my riding has brought it to my attention that they are in need of assistance under the P.F.R.A. in the form of small water projects. We have never had such assistance in any part of my riding, but the time has now arrived when we feel it should be extended to cover an area 50 to 100 miles farther north than is now the case. It varies from east to west according to whether you are on the east side or the west. As you go farther west it extends farther north. It would have to extend possibly 50 miles farther north on the east side and 100 miles farther north on the west side in order to be effective. It is not my intention to delay the committee, but I thought this matter should be brought to the attention of the government. I know the minister is quite conversant with this situation, but many hon. members who are being asked to vote on the proposition as to whether this area should be extended are not acquainted with the facts. I am making these comments in order to present the point of view of the people of that area, and to assure the committee that we are not asking for something that will not be returned tenfold.
In conclusion I would like the minister, if he would be so kind, to tell us what he thinks we may expect in the future with respect to the extension of this area, and how soon we may expect it. I know my people in Meadow Lake will be greatly interested.

I think I explained earlier in the session that two bills we had intimated would be brought down this year would not be brought down until next session. One of

those bills is based upon P.F.R.A. in the west; the other is based upon the marshlands operations in the maritimes. The one is based upon the need to procure and conserve water; the other is based upon the need to control water. It has been said here from time to time that- we should extend P.F.R.A. right across Canada. Well, that would be difficult, because after all that has to do with prairie farm rehabilitation and has particular application to irrigation, stock watering dams and dugouts such as have been described by the last few speakers. On the other hand a considerable portion of the work in which this government might assist in eastern Canada would be in connection with rescuing land from the ocean, as is done in the maritimes by means of dikes. The same thing probably would be necessary at certain points along the St. Lawrence river, and even at other points around the great lakes.
Another activity which might be undertaken is the development of the black marshes in eastern Canada. There are such marshes on many farms in Ontario. I remember there was one on the farm my grandfather homesteaded when he came to Canada a hundred years ago. That black marsh is still there, and I remember that we used to spend our Sunday afternoons going down and pulling livestock out of that bog. Mr. Hepburn, who used to be premier of Ontario, has developed one of these black marshes on his own farm; that is where he grows the onions we hear so much about. It is one of the best producing areas in Ontario, requiring the work of as many as sixty men in the summer months, though a few years ago it was more or less of an eyesore on his farm. His cattle and horses used to get bogged down there, too; but he drained that swamp. As a result he has one of the finest fire fighting systems I have ever seen on a farm. The water is piped into his buildings, and then is taken below his place where it feeds one of the finest lakes I have ever seen. He does not have to go somewhere else in Ontario to find a summer resort; he has one just outside his door. That sort of thing on a farm makes farming really worth while, and there are black marshes like that all over eastern Canada, particularly in Ontario, which can be developed into highly productive areas.
We think work of that kind could be assisted from Ottawa over the years to come. So the legislation we intend to bring down next session will include two bills, one of which will provide for an extension of the work in the west while the other will deal with work in the east. I think I can say both those bills will be brought down next session.

The projects on the prairies are being undertaken in much the same way as those under vote No. 38 and vote No. 42. Those are the two votes that were put in the estimates first about 1947. They were put in deliberately, because we were not then in a position to proceed with the legislation I have mentioned. We thought these works ought to be moved along, and that in the meantime we should get some experience in handling them; and we have had considerable experience. These votes I think will be brought under the new legislation, but it is sometimes thought that in this work we are doing on the prairie we just go out there and do the work; that is not true. In connection with these dugouts we only pay 4J cents per yard for the removal of the earth. It often costs three times that to move the earth, and the farmer payg it himself.
In other cases where we have put in water for irrigation, as for example the Swift Current project, the provincial government actually promotes the irrigation of the land, that is the utilization of the water, and the farmers themselves pay a considerable part of the cost. Practically all we do is put in a dam, and then put in a ditch to distribute the water to surrounding points. From that point it is taken up by the provincial government and by the farmers, just in the same way as we started in the Pemberton valley in British Columbia. The first project we had there we started because it was a returned soldier settlement. I was taken out there and looked at it, and I thought it was one of the finest valleys I had seen and could be made habitable. It was being flooded every spring, and these returned men were practically being put off their land. The government did spend a considerable amount of money there, and spent it directly, in order to determine whether anything could be done. We wanted to get to a point where we knew it could be done. We knew the province had land there and if it could be taken care of an arrangement might be made. We entered into an arrangement with the province whereby we paid one-third, the province paid one-third, and the farmers paid one-third. We feel that this administration will have been improved by the time the bill is brought down, and we can bring all that under this legislation.

speechtext: The house resumed from Friday, May 26, consideration of the motion of Mr. Knowles for the second reading of Bill No. 13, to provide for the jurisdiction of the Exchequer Court of Canada in matters of divorce.

subtopic: EXCHEQUER COURT TO HAVE JURISDICTION IN ACTIONS ORIGINATING IN QUEBEC AND NEWFOUNDLAND
speechtext:

subtopic: EXCHEQUER COURT TO HAVE JURISDICTION IN ACTIONS ORIGINATING IN QUEBEC AND NEWFOUNDLAND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, for the second time I am availing myself of my right, as a free man and as a representative of a Quebec constituency, to discuss a divorce bill. Indeed, whatever aspects it may deal with, it still is a divorce bill.
The hon. member would like to have referred to the exchequer court those bills that are now being dealt with by the Senate. Even if such a measure did in effect tend to 
rid us of a disgraceful list of bills submitted for our approval periodically, we cannot agree with him. Nor can we agree with his claims that reference of those divorce bills to the exchequer court would not set up, in so far as Quebec and Newfoundland are concerned, a divorce court. On the contrary, I believe it would set up such a court for Quebec and Newfoundland. My hon. friend from Newfoundland has explained the situation very well when he gave the reasons why they had not agreed to this change proposed by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles).
I have here an article written by a Quebec Jesuit, Reverend Father Louis C. de Lery, an expert on such matters. He mentions several reasons why Quebec opposes any change in the present procedure. Father de Lery states:
Quebec has never recognized divorce. When our ancestors came to this country over three centuries ago, they had their own religion and their own laws, which recognized the indissolubility of marriage. This indissoluble character was recognized by the organic law of 1774. In 1865, the union parliament sanctioned in Lower Canada the use of our civil code, recently consolidated. Section 185 of that code asserts the indissoluble character of the marriage ties. Again, according to the British North America Act (1867) the provinces have exclusive legislative authority in the matter of civil rights. Those rights are contained in our civil code.
In transferring the authority in the matter of divorce to the exchequer court, we would infringe upon provincial autonomy, because the provinces have exclusive rights to legislate in that field.
The constitution of 1867 therefore sanctioned our civil code, and in section 185, recognized the indissolubility of marriage as law of the province.
To those who claim that regard for the minority groups of the province of Quebec and of Newfoundland entitles them to divorce courts, I reply that the establishment of such courts in the province of Quebec would affect not only minorities but everyone else.
According to the Act of 1867, the dominion parliament is empowered to legislate with reference to marriage and divorce while the provinces have the exclusive right to pass legislation concerning marriage within their respective provincial sphere and to organize provincial and federal courts dealing with divorce. However, by entrusting any court with the duty of hearing divorce cases, the federal parliament would violate the indissolubility of marriage recognized in our province.
As is pointed out by Father de Lery, we have, for the past three hundred years,

believed in the indissolubility of the marriage ties. This conviction does not stem from bigotry or narrow-mindedness; we hold it because, knowing marriage to be indissoluble, we refuse to open the door to those who would strike at our democratic institution by weakening the family, the foundation of our national and social structure.
Other attempts have already been made in this direction, in order to make it easier to obtain a divorce. If the bill introduced by the hon. member from Winnipeg North Centre were to pass, divorce would, of course, be much easier, since this would be a general act that applied to all. However, I am of the opinion that we cannot pass it without changing the British North America Act.
I have here a quotation from a speech delivered in this house on March 24, 1944, by the present Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent). The quotation reads as follows:
In Quebec not only is there no jurisdiction to deal with divorce, but there is a pre-confederation law, which was continued in force by the British North America Act, and which will remain in force until this parliament chooses to deal with it, as it has jurisdiction to do under section 91 of the British North America Act. This pre-confederation law declares that marriage is dissolved only by the natural death of one of the spouses. No matter what jurisdiction you set up, so long as that is the law of the province, no divorce could be granted by any court.
Consequently, if we were to pass the bill introduced by our hon. friend from Winnipeg North Centre, we would be obliged to set up an entirely new general law which would grant those provinces that are opposed to divorce, Quebec and Newfoundland, greater facilities to that end. Such a law would provide changes not approved by everybody and would therefore create new problems from the constitutional point of view, in regard to the rights enjoyed by the provinces and the federal government.
Another minister of justice, the Hon. Charles Doherty, stated in 1916:
The parties come here asking for it, just as they come with other private bills when they want to get something that the general law of the country does not give them. And it is precisely because the general law of the country says: once you are married you cannot marry again while your consort is alive, that when one wants to be relieved of the operation of that general law, he comes to the parliament of Canada and asks for a law for himself.
Then, if the power to grant divorce was taken away from the Senate, we would commit the very mistake to which the minister of justice, the Hon. Mr. Doherty, was referring. On the subject of our belief in the indissolubility of marriage, the Right Hon. Mr. St. Laurent said on March 24, 1944:
There are applications for legislation which come before this parliament, and where divorces are
Divorce Jurisdiction
enacted. This is not a matter of right; no one has any right to a parliamentary divorce. That is a special legislative grant that is made under special circumstances revealed by the investigation carried on before a committee.
And to those who ask: "What about the minority?" we would answer:
Courts cannot be set up only for those who feel they might use them. To set up a divorce court for Quebec would in effect give to the people of the province the right to apply to it. If a court exists, anyone who feels he has been wronged may apply to such court for relief. Setting up a court would be tantamount to recognition of divorce.
So that, if it were passed, the hon. member's bill would in effect set up a new court for the province of Quebec and Newfoundland, and divorce would thereby be recognized. For this reason, we from the province of Quebec are opposed to the passage of this bill.
In making it easier to secure divorce we can only fall into a kind of exaggeration that has distressed other countries and in respect of which I have given figures.
You may say that we have not yet reached a point where divorce is granted with excessive liberality, but I do believe that such a stage would necessarily be reached if we go at it step by step. If we don't resist the manoeuvres and the requests of those who seek to make divorce easier, we will make a step forward today and another one tomorrow. But I don't believe that this is intended by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre. What he wants is merely to free the Senate and the House of Commons from all those divorce bills. I understand his intentions. However, he will never reach his objective. On the contrary, he will lead us into another mess and we will never be able to get out of it, because he cannot understand our way of thinking in Quebec or the way of thinking in the new province of Newfoundland. I have already quoted figures on juvenile delinquency in a country where divorce is free.
I was quoting the example of Russia. I am aware that by referring divorces cases to the exchequer court the provinces would still retain the right to legislate in the matter of forsaken children. I think that children should not be left in the care of parents who are so little concerned about their duty.
Soviet Russia gave much freedom in the matter of divorce. In fact, even Lenin's wife realized one day that thousands and thousands of children,-I believe there were millions,- roamed about after being forsaken by their divorced parents. Of course, they were roaming about the streets of Moscow and other

Divorce Jurisdiction
cities in Soviet Russia, stealing, attacking and even killing passers-by to such an extent that when the so-called popular commissaries in Russia realized the situation they were compelled to introduce restrictions and to amend the divorce laws and even the laws concerning abortion.
In addition, they had to enact a very restrictive law and to inflict upon these vagrant children severe penalties in order to eliminate this public menace. They had to turn back. They had embarked on a very costly experiment. They had to depart from too easy divorces and come back to normal.
When I stated in this house that this experiment could be used by the Russians against the democracies, I believe I was perfectly right. When the family is broken by divorce, it becomes an easy prey to communism, which thus creeps into our democratic community.
As a result of that experience, there is no doubt that communists, knowing where the weaknesses are and how they can best spread their doctrines, will try to impress upon our modern democracies that there can be no harm in facilitating divorce.
Those who are caught in the trap are surely not aware how greatly the stability of the family can strengthen the whole democratic structure.
Quebec's position in the matter of divorce is sufficiently clear and firm, I believe. Therefore, those that wish to help that province or seem to think that dissolution of the marriage ties should be facilitated, will know exactly where we stand in this connection, since our position has been clearly defined.
Here is an article taken from the Toronto Daily Star of June 12, 1950. I shall read it all, because I think it is excellent. It deals with an opinion expressed by communist Russia on the matter of divorces imposed upon foreigners who marry Russian women.
(Text):
I hope I will not be out of order if I quote an article from the Toronto Daily Star which shows what can happen if we do not take the necessary precautions to prevent an increase in the dissolution of marriage or against the providing of additional facilities for the obtaining of divorce. This article which supports the argument I have expounded in French reads:
[Mr. Gauthier (Portneuf).l
The nullification in England by the appeal court of a marriage in Russia between a British citizen and a Russian woman serves as a reminder that the soviet union, although she professes to be above racial discrimination and to have respect for human rights and personality, possesses the narrowest and cruelest policy in the world with respect to marriage and emigration.
The soviet forbids marriage between her citizens and foreigners. In that respect she is in a class by herself. Worse still, she refuses to permit the Russian wives of peoples of other nationalities to leave soviet territory.
In 1947 when a Canadian bacteriologist who had been in the Canadian legation at Moscow as military attache sought to bring his Russian wife to America, he having been transferred to Detroit, the soviet government refused to let her go.
Vyshinsky, now Russian foreign minister, explained that this was no indication of racial prejudice on the part of the soviet union; that it was "the duty of a Russian woman to produce soviet children, not children for the Canadian government." He also said, and this was nearer the true explanation: "Women talk too much and give the wrong impression of the soviet union."
As I have stated already in my brief remarks in French, they realize the weaknesses in their system of dissolving marriages because they know that that in turn breaks up the basic family cell. The article continues:
It is believed that mere than 800 persons who claim United States citizenship have been denied permission to leave Russia. In addition, 350 Russian women who married western soldiers or diplomats have been held by their homeland. During the past 17 years only 50 women who wished to stay with their American husbands were permitted to leave. At least 15 British husbands have tried in vain to get their Russian wives out of the soviet union. Many hardships, much distress of mind and broken marriages have resulted.
I realize that in quoting that article I am not entirely in order and I thank the hon. member fpr Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) for not having raised a point of order about it. I realize that he is sincere in introducing this bill, and while it may not provide additional facilities for the obtaining of divorce it does create a new court for divorce in Quebec, the exchequer court.

speechtext:
Just to show how far this can go, just to show how it has reached the point where it can be referred to as a national disgrace, I should like to quote from another article in the Toronto Daily Star of May 2, 1950, as follows:
Riverside, California, May 2-If she follows her schedule, Mrs. George W. Ettinger soon will divorce for the fourth time a husband who has spent 18 of his last 22 years in various prisons.
Ettinger, 37, is headed for San Quentin today after being convicted on bad cheque charges.
Probation officers told the court yesterday that each time he has gone to prison, his wife has divorced him and married someone else. But upon Ettinger's release, she always has shed her interim husband to remarry him.
That is the kind of record they are creating in the United States and I would not like to see Canadian parents give their children a similar example. That is why we always oppose additional facilities for the obtaining of divorce. I am sure also that my hon. friends from Newfoundland would not want to change their present procedure.

speakeroldname: Mr. W. J. Browne (St. John's West):
subtopic: EXCHEQUER COURT TO HAVE JURISDICTION IN ACTIONS ORIGINATING IN QUEBEC AND NEWFOUNDLAND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I believe my position with regard to a bill of this kind is well known because I have spoken on this subject in this house before. However, I feel that I would not be doing justice to the people I represent if I did not say something about it. I think I understand the motive that actuated the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) when he introduced this bill. I am sure he did it with the best of intentions. Hon. members may not be familiar with the proviso in the bill that when an application for divorce is made to the exchequer court the court may decline to grant it when it is satisfied that the petitioner or the plaintiff has committed either adultery or acts of cruelty toward his spouse. I think the chief motive actuating the sponsor of the bill was to rid parliament, and especially the House of Commons, of the embarrassment that comes to it so frequently during a session when a large group of divorce bills is brought before it and we are faced with saying yes or no to granting the dissolution of these marriages. I think there is a great division of opinion among hon. members as to what should be done about divorce. So far as I am concerned, I regard marriage as indissoluble. Once it has been properly formed it is indissoluble. I think hon. members are fairly familiar
Divorce Jurisdiction
with the arguments advanced by Catholics as to the only grounds upon which annulment may be granted.
As has been explained, there is of course a distinction between annulment and divorce; annulment applies where no proper valid marriage has taken place. Divorce occurs when there has been a valid marriage, and parliament, by a right which it assumes to itself, intervenes and says that the valid marriage shall no longer be a valid marriage because one of the parties thereto has violated his agreement.
We are all prepared to recognize that marriage is a very solemn event in anyone's life. It should be very carefully considered before being entered into, and it seems to me in many cases that come before the courts the trouble between the parties has arisen because they married too hastily. I have read some of the evidence in the cases that have come before us, and I find that the people did not know each other properly before they went through the marriage ceremony. Again, when they have been married and have lived together some trouble has arisen. Sometimes you will read evidence where one party has left the other and never gone back, and the other party has made no effort at reconciliation. Nobody has intervened to try to bring about a reconciliation.
Therefore I say all hon. members are faced with the question of how we regard marriage. I am a little astonished that the sponsor of the bill, who I believe is a clergyman in private life, should be the one to introduce a measure of this kind even though it has as its purpose the sending of divorce cases to the exchequer court. If we regard the marriage contract, as the words of the ceremony put it, "for better or for worse, for richer or for poorer until death do us part," I cannot understand how anyone can reasonably argue that such a contract can be dissolved even by parliament.
One must regard marriage as a sacred thing. It was instituted by Our Lord himself. We are Christians, and therefore we ought not to interfere with it. There have been cases where marriages have gone on the rocks and people have been forced to live apart, but is it not better that they should live apart than that they should bring about a condition of society that might mean its ruin? I suppose the Roman state was the greatest state the world has ever seen. Rome was mistress of the world without a rival for hundreds of years. The material, literary, artistic and architectural accomplishments of Rome have not been equalled by any other

Divorce Jurisdiction
state. We may build greater things but I doubt whether we have built the better things, things that after 2,000 years will still win the admiration of those who will be alive at that time as the art and architecture of Greece and Rome still win our admiration. Yet that society, strong as it was, was destroyed.
It seems to me we are making all kinds of provisions for the material happiness of people. We are providing family allowances to help families overcome the difficulties that they encounter. We are providing for their old age, and in spite of all these material advantages,.that people have today we find that many of them are not a bit happier, that some marriages are not being observed in the way that they should be, and that divorce is becoming more frequent.
In the debate that took place on the motion introduced by the hon. member for Spadina (Mr. Croll) during the first part of the session I pointed out-and I think he recognized- that divorce has been increasing, and until the last year or so was increasing at a very rapid rate. It was not a question of two or three extra a year but two or three hundred. In the space of fifty years or so the number of persons seeking divorce has risen from almost zero into thousands. At the beginning of the century there were very few people applying for divorce, and in some of the provinces there were none. Therefore when you provide more methods by which divorces can be granted and make it easier to secure a divorce you are going to have more divorces. That was the purpose of the hon. member's motion and he was good enough to withdraw it.
I think we all agree that, in addition to material benefits to the family, we would like to see spiritual benefits as well. We would like to see families happier and marriages more enduring. Therefore we have to consider what the purpose of marriage is. It is not only the procreation of children but also the spiritual attachment that exists and the spiritual benefits that come to each of the spouses when they have gone through the marriage ceremony. There is a complementary and natural relation between husband and wife, wife and husband, and parents and children, so that in a normal family there should be children. There will be continuity of the tradition of goodness and a way of living passed on from parent to child. When we have divorce the continuity is broken, and from our own experience we know many families where that has taken place and the children have become more than orphans. When parents marry again we get even greater complications. That may not seem to be very

serious at the present time because the number of divorces granted in Canada only reaches about 6,000 or 7,000 a year, but in the United States, the number is seven times as great today in proportion to population as it is in Canada. We can feel confident that the rate of divorce is going to increase in Canada as well.
I think the time has come for us to realize that we must face the question of whether we are going to permit divorce in Canada, and not only the question of whether we are going to make it more convenient by having divorces dealt with by the exchequer court. Are we going to abandon that system? Is every hon. member really satisfied that divorce is a good thing in itself? I do not suppose many people in this house really think it is a good thing; they are happy in their married life anc^ would like to see their children happy in the same way. I do not suppose many of them would care to see their children suffer the public scandal and unhappiness that so often follow divorce. I suggest, therefore, that we should see that our young people take greater care in the selection of a partner before marriage, and that if difficulties arise afterwards provision should be made for counsel and advice to help overcome those difficulties. I have already mentioned the fact that many times I have seen people who never wanted to speak to each other again, .but who, after a little time had elapsed and as a result of good advice, became reconciled and lived happily together again.
In my opinion it is not possible for two people to live together and always be happy. They are bound to have difficulties; but with the proper attitude they will be given the necessary strength to overcome them.
When Admiral Byrd was going to the south pole he refused to take a companion with him because he said it would be only a short time before they would be quarrelling. He spent six months in isolation rather than have a companion because he appreciated the problems that would arise. When a husband and wife have trouble of that kind there are ways of overcoming it. At the university of Notre Dame there is a priest, Father O'Brien, who was once called by a family where a terrible dispute was going on. He found that the cause was nothing really serious, and at that time made a resolution that from then on every time he performed the marriage ceremony he would make the parties promise never to say an angry word to each other. For thirty-five years he carried out that resolve. After the wedding ceremony was over he would take the parties aside and make each promise the other never to say an angry word. I know that is a very hard promise to keep, but he says it has worked.

In my view divorce is one of the great evils of our times. What we should do is try to build up a good family life and family solidarity, as the last speaker said. I believe we would be better occupied if we spent our time looking for ways to improve the conditions of family life, perhaps on a higher plane than has been the case in the past. There is no doubt that family allowances and old age pensions have removed some of the economic causes that led to divorce, and have helped families to get along better. In my view there are other things that would also help, and I believe we would be better occupied if we spend our time considering them instead of considering ways of making divorce easier.
As far as my province is concerned, we have not asked for this legislation. As a matter of fact, in the constitution of Newfoundland as it existed prior to confederation there was a provision that the governor should not permit a divorce bill to be passed. I am not sure, but it seems to me questionable whether persons resident in Newfoundland can be divorced. It could be done only on the authority of parliament; and that brings me to another point.

That was the evidence upon which the

divorces were granted by the other place; and of course when those bills came here the evidence was not read at all. As far as the matter of evidence is concerned, I have no doubt that the method proposed by the hon. member would be much sounder from the legal point of view, but I am afraid it would have the effect of making divorces easier to obtain.
This bill does not touch the fundamental, basic issue at all, as to whether or not we should have divorce. I am opposed to divorce in any form, and for that reason I am opposed to this bill.

subtopic: EXCHEQUER COURT TO HAVE JURISDICTION IN ACTIONS ORIGINATING IN QUEBEC AND NEWFOUNDLAND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, apart from the sponsor of the bill, the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles), all those who have spoken have been in opposition to it. My purpose in speaking this evening is to offer support, and I shall give my reasons for doing so as I go along. I have been a member of this house for more than ten years, and this is the first occasion on which I have uttered a word with respect to our method of handling divorce cases. Whenever the opportunity presented itself to vote against our procedure, I have done so. When I came here over ten years ago and witnessed the way we handled divorce cases from Quebec and Prince Edward Island, I was amazed. After having been here a while and witnessed that procedure during several sessions, I became shocked. Now, in the course of my eleventh year, I am completely disgusted.
I should like to _ stress one extremely important fact in connection with this bill. In no sense does it broaden the grounds for divorce. It seemed to me that the hon. member for St. John's West (Mr. Browne), consciously or otherwise, conveyed the impression that the grounds for divorce were being broadened by this legislation, but that is not the case. As a matter of fact I can easily appreciate that divorce might be made more difficult as a result of transferring jurisdiction to the Exchequer Court of Canada. Perhaps I should say at this point that I dislike divorce just as much as any hon. member of this house. I think it is appalling when one examines the statistics in Canada, and learns the extent to which divorce is increasing within our nation. Thank goodness it is not as bad as it is in the United States where divorce, in my opinion, has made marriage nothing more than legalized adultery. I am not too certain that transferring the jurisdiction to the Exchequer Court of Canada is the best method of dealing with the question, but certainly there is no doubt in my mind that it is preferable to the method which we are applying at the present time.

Divorce Jurisdiction
I would be the last one to offer any suggestions or any hints that hon. gentlemen in the other place do not do the best possible job, having regard to all the circumstances. But, Mr. Speaker, not so long ago we had occasion to discuss in this chamber the work of the other chamber. The thought that entered my mind at the time was that if we would not tie them up by forcing them to deal with over 300 divorce cases in the course of one session, possibly they would be in a better position to render more effective service on behalf of the Dominion of Canada.
Mr. Speaker, I have a clipping from the Montreal Gazette of June 13, and I think I should refer to it because it is extremely significant. It is under the dateline, Ottawa, June 12, and reads as follows:
The Senate committee on divorce presented its final report of the session today and with a last flourish, protested again the system that annually brings hundreds of divorce seekers to the doorstep of parliament.
The report then refers to the fact that Senator W. N. Aseltine, sixty-four year old Rosetown lawyer and wheat farmer and father of five children, who has been a member for sixteen years and chairman for ten, now finds it necessary to resign. Here is a further paragraph from the report:
The report disclosed that in granting divorces to 235 Quebec petitioners and 5 from Newfoundland- other provinces have their own divorce courts-the dominion treasury would get $47,330 in fees. But it indicated the work of hearing petitions was getting tougher every year and it wasn't worth the money.
In concluding the report states:
Your committee regrets that parliament has not yet seen fit to solve the problem of parliamentary divorce by setting up suitable tribunals before which these numerous cases from Quebec and Newfoundland can be heard.
It is to be hoped that something will be done in that regard in the near future because members of the divorce committee are compelled, under the present set-up, to spend the greater part of their time in hearing evidence, thus leaving little or no time for the performance of their other important duties.
Mr. Speaker, I believe that as long as we leave that growing burden on their doorstep we have little justification for criticizing them if they do not happen to do as much as we believe they should in other spheres of activity.
I should like to quote one more paragraph from this article:
Senator Robertson said whether or not another method of dealing with divorces from Quebec and Newfoundland could be found remained to be seen. But at the moment this was a responsibility of the Senate and he believed Senators should be willing to shoulder their responsibility.
I hasten to add that I believe they have shouldered the responsibility, but I certainly believe it is a responsibility that should no longer rest upon them.

In summarizing let me repeat that I am as much opposed to divorce as any other member in this house. I repeat also that I think the statistics which are available to all should present cause for alarm, but certainly in imposing upon parliament this onerous task we are doing nothing to cause any decrease in the number of divorce applications from those two provinces. We are becoming a joke, as it were, in the method by which we deal with these petitions. Today we pick them up in blocks, whereas ten years ago we at least gave some consideration to each individual divorce case. We have now reached the stage where we say, shall section 1 of a group of twenty-five or thirty divorce bills carry? Shall section 2 of a group of twenty-five or thirty divorce bills carry? I ask hon. members what could be more ridiculous than that?
Someone may say that these cases are thoroughly considered by the divorce committee, and that is true. Some say that the committee on miscellaneous private bills goes through the evidence and makes recommendations. That is true, but we cannot escape the responsibility that arises from the fact that these divorces cannot become final unless they are approved by this house, and it is the method by which this house handles these divorce cases that I am protesting very vigorously. Certainly, sir, in speaking thus I am speaking for myself. I have not consulted my colleagues. I do not know what they think about this matter, but certainly I have no hesitation in advancing my personal support of the bill now before us.

I should like to ask the minister a question in connection with the Bow River Development and Irrigation Company. Have final arrangements been made for the government to take over that company, or are negotiations still being conducted?

So far as the discussions with the company are concerned, and the discussions with the provincial government, final arrangements have been made. As my hon. friend knows, these companies went into receivership, and the two companies have not been cleared from the records over in Great Britain. We thought that would be accomplished by April 1, but there have been some delays on the other side. We do not feel we should proceed with any development work until the titles are clear. I do not believe there will be any trouble about it, but it is a matter of delay. We regret the delay, but we cannot do anything about it.

What I object to is that over a year ago it was announced that the company had agreed to sell to the dominion government. At that time most of us were anxious that that should be done so that we could get ahead with the irrigation projects in Alberta, especially west of Medicine Hat. However, another year has gone by, and nothing has been done; that is two years of inaction since the election. Surely they are not going to wait until another election comes around before they tell us that they are going to do something in connection with the scheme. May I say we in that corner of the province have listened to these promises for years and years. We are still listening to them. Canada is lagging far behind in irrigation in comparison with other countries. I am going to put on record what some of the other countries have done in connection with irrigation. In India they have 60,100,000 acres under irrigation. In China they have 47,500,000 under irrigation; in the United States they have 21 million; in Russia they have eight million; in Japan, 7,600,000; in Egypt, 6,500,000; in France, 5,720,000; in Mexico, 5,700,000; in Italy, 4,900,000; in Iraq, four million; in Spain, 3,500,000; in Java, three million; in Chile, 2,970,000; in Brazil, 2,200,000; in Morocco, 1,500,000, and in Canada we have one million acres under irrigation.
How much have they in Babylonia?

In so far as irrigation is concerned, we are at the bottom of the list of these countries. In Alberta we who have suffered one loss after another are beginning to realize that the government is not very anxious to put in irrigation.
Supply-Agriculture
I want to refer to a very important speech that was made in this house on May 31 by the Prime Minister of Pakistan. What he had to say certainly applied to this country. I am reading from page 3043 of Hansard:
But democracy, in Pakistan or elsewhere, is of little use to the common man unless its advantages are made available to him in his daily life and his standard of living is raised at least to a level which gives him a substantial stake in the way of life which he has chosen for himself.
We are fully conscious of this, and consider it our foremost duty to develop the resources of our country at the greatest possible speed. Even in the days of our greatest anxieties we were able to go ahead with this task, and though much remains to be done we are glad that we have been able to revive our trade, to plan the development of our irrigation, the expansion and modernization of our agriculture and the utilization of our power resources: to keep our budgets balanced and to throw the gates wide open to private enterprise in our industrial development. For this task there is nothing more essential to us and nothing that we could or do desire more passionately than peace.
The Prime Minister of Pakistan realizes, as I am sure we do, that we must advance the development of our resources. We in southeastern Alberta, an area which this year has been hit by one dust storm after another, and an area in which crop conditions at the present time are not good-as the minister knows, the whole of the province is only 57 per cent of normal, which is a serious situation because when the whole of the province is 57 per cent of normal one realizes that the southern part is the driest and especially the southeastern part-look upon this irrigation development as something that we want to see go ahead. Nothing has been done on the Canada Land and Irrigation Company or the Bow river development last year, and nothing will be done this year. We are still waiting for someone over in London, England, to agree to the price that the government wants to pay for the land. I think it is absolutely ridiculous, and we are still-
It would be ridiculous if it were true; it is not.
The minister make a remark. I did not hear what he said.
I said:	"It would be ridiculous if it were true; it is not."
It certainly is true. I will be glad to sit down if the minister wants to tell me what is going on, and what is going on in connection with the development of that project.
You would not listen, anyway.

I will listen. I will listen to the minister at any time if he can tell me where there is any development going on in

Supply-Agriculture
that project whereby the cities of Redcliff and Medicine Hat are going to benefit by the extension of that irrigation project. I will be glad to sit down and listen to him, but nothing has been done. The minister knows as well as I do that nothing is being done.

No, I do not. My hon. friend and his friend up there, who is one of the local members, are spending considerable time spreading rumours that keep the people more or less worked up about it all the time. By coming here and saying that nothing is being done about it he is obstructing it all he can.

I certainly disagree with everything the minister has said, because I do not know to whom he refers as the local member. If he refers to me I am certainly willing to debate it with him at any time; but so far as talking to some local member is concerned, I do not know who the local member is. Perhaps the minister knows more than I do about what is going on.
You know all about it.

If the minister knows I wish he would tell us. It would overcome the worry, and many people are worried today. There are letters in the Medicine Hat News almost every week wondering what is happening to our irrigation project. A big debate went on between the Medicine Hat News and the Lethbridge Herald about bringing water down from the St. Mary dam, which I stayed out of completely. These letters are appearing every week. People want to know what is going on. I would certainly like to hear what is being done on the Bow river development scheme.

Perhaps this is the item on which I should say a few words. Hon. members will recall that in the house last year I told of the sad plight of Regina city owing to the government in the early days having located it in the wrong place. I gave hon. members a picture of the rapidly falling water table; I told of the difficulties we had in obtaining a supply of water and of having to go to the Saskatchewan river to seek one.
Last year a conference was arranged between the provincial authorities, the city of Regina and the dominion government in Ottawa. At that conference the city was willing and said it was able to pay one-third of the cost of bringing a water supply to Regina. The provincial government denied any responsibility. I remember the Minister of Trade and Commerce, who was at the conference, stating that had the provincial government been willing to assume its
[Mr. Wylie.1
responsibility he would have found it very difficult to have refused to assume the other one-third.
That conference came to naught. We went back home and this summer we studied our problem and carried on, and again we came back for another conference. There is one principle I want to make clear, namely, that the first responsibility rests upon any municipality for a water supply of its own. First, the municipality, then the provincial government and lastly the dominion government is responsible. If it is beyond the means of the municipality to supply its own water it can get assistance from the others. But the provincial government is one that is next responsible for that assistance. This whole issue is being obscured today because it is being charged by provincial authorities that when I was seeking election in Regina City I claimed that I alone would get the city of Regina a water supply. I am not quite equal to that; but I wish to say today that out of the last conference has come an offer to the city of Regina and to the province of Saskatchewan that the dominion government will place water in Buffalo Pound lake, which is about forty miles from Regina. That means that the dominion government will bring water from the Saskatchewan river to Buffalo Pound lake, which is north of Moose Jaw, and about forty miles west of Regina.
Here they offer to maintain a supply of water until such time as the dam is built at Outlook, and water will flow by gravity down the Qu'Appelle river. They offer to put it into Buffalo Pound lake, and stand the cost of maintaining the water supply there, but I do not think they have gone far enough. That would probably mean an initial outlay by the dominion government of $650,000 or $700,000. There would be a yearly outlay for keeping it there by pumping of about $12,000 or $15,000-perhaps even $20,000.
But that water is not being kept there for Regina and Moose Jaw alone. It is being kept there to supply irrigation projects, stockwatering projects, and irrigation all down the valley to Brandon. So that by doing this there is not a great deal being done for Regina and Moose Jaw. What they are doing is saying that they will replace any water out of Buffalo Pound lake that Regina and Moose Jaw will use. As urban municipalities Regina and Moose Jaw are perfectly entitled to go to Buffalo Pound lake, take all the water from there and leave the farmers high and dry.
However I think, though I wish to thank the government for what it has done in assuring us of a supply of water, and while

the people of my city are vigorous and willing to face problems-I repeat that-I think the cost is too high. The second step of that project is to bring the water out of Buffalo Pound lake up about 175 feet to filtration beds, and from there it can be taken to Regina and Moose Jaw. That will entail another expenditure of about four million dollars. Surely hon. members sitting in the House of Commons this evening do not want to see Regina and Moose Jaw have an insufficient water supply.
Hon. members will agree with me when I say that it is the duty of the dominion government to pump that water out of Buffalo Pound lake and bring it up to the filtration beds, and say, "Here is your fresh water supply. You can pipe it in yourselves." That is what should be done, and that is what I am asking the minister to have done, if at all possible.

Mr. Chairman, there are one or two comments I should like to make on this item. If the Minister of Agriculture meant what he said before six o'clock, it might mean a good deal to western Canada. Because if I understood him correctly he said that next week, when he goes west, if a suitable agreement can be signed with the provinces construction work might be started next year on the south Saskatchewan irrigation project.
I am disappointed of course that it is not being started this year. But if it is actually going ahead next year the minister will have accomplished a good deal, and I shall then be happy to congratulate him. There is one word of admonition I should like to express. I understand the agreement he will probably try to make with Saskatchewan will be based upon the master agreement of the St. Mary project, which he made with Alberta. If that is so, I hope he will not be too difficult with the Saskatchewan government. Alberta might be able to sign an expensive agreement because of their oil wells and oil leases, but Saskatchewan may not be able to do quite so well.
I hope the minister will take all that into consideration when he is drawing up this proposed agreement with Saskatchewan. 1 do not know whether eastern members realize just how badly the south Saskatchewan irrigation project is needed, but I can say I was in western Canada last week. Between Moose Jaw and Saskatoon I had an opportunity to look down from an aeroplane, but could not see the ground because of the dust that was blowing. The tragedy of the situation is that through the middle of the dust bowl area the south Saskatchewan river flows, and it hardly
Supply-Agriculture
seems sensible that we as a parliament should permit that condition to continue. The water is there, flowing out into Hudson bay.
If we would put a dam there, or several dams, and utilize that water we could eliminate many of these P.F.R.A. and P.F.A.A. expenditures which we now have. So far as the statement made just now by the hon. member for Regina City is concerned, he pointed out that the Buffalo Pound lake project would cost too much. I do not think the people of Regina or Moose Jaw feel that the federal government made a proper offer recently at all. I speak from memory, but my recollection is that the federal government offered to pay about half a million, while the total cost was five or six million. The mayor of Regina expressed great disappointment in that.
I do not think that the Buffalo Pound project is a proper solution. If the minister and the government would proceed with the south Saskatchewan irrigation project next year, Regina and Moose Jaw would get a proper water supply and we would have the whole area irrigated. I must emphasize again that this is not the only western project, because if the west has another recession, or if they hit another drought period, the eastern manufacturers who sell merchandise in that part of the country will suffer, as well as anybody else. I say again to the minister that if he does what he promised about this south Saskatchewan irrigation project, then he will go down in history as a great westerner.
