Mr. Chairman, some time ago I joined with many hon. members of this house in expressing my good wishes to the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration upon his appointment to this new office and, like other hon. members of this house, I looked forward to his first official address. On April 21 the minister outlined the departmental policy. I have always had much regard for the minister's ability and integrity; I thought that his appointment was a mark of recognition that was well deserved and I looked forward to hearing the government's immigration policy. I must confess that like other hon. members I was disappointed.
On reading the minister's speech I found that he said what every other political party has been saying since 1945. As a matter of fact, he did not go one step further. He said that he was in favour of immigration, but as I read Hansard I find that every party in this house is in favour of immigration. The Tories were in favour of it; the Conservatives were in favour of it; the Progressives were in favour of it; the C.C.F. were in favour of it; the socialists were in favour of it; the Social Crediters were in favour of it, and I gather that the Liberals were in favour of it. That seems to be the signal for real action.
Yet to date we have heard very little about any new immigration policy enunciated by this government. The minister said in his statement that the country has benefited in the past from immigration. That proposition has been around for a long time because I have been hearing it ever since I can remember and I imagine my father heard it also. The minister said also that this country could support a larger number of people than we have at the present time. That has been around for some fifty years. We have believed in that. Then the minister repeated the words of Mr. King, as prime minister, in 1947 as follows:
The policy of the government Is to foster the growth of the population of Canada by the encouragement of immigration. The government will seek by legislation, regulation and vigorous administration to ensure the careful selection and permanent settlement of such numbers of immigrants as can advantageously be absorbed in the national economy.

I think it will be admitted that that is not a new policy or a very forthright one. In fact I am inclined to agree that it is not a policy at all. The best you can say for that statement is that it is a pious hope, except for the use of the word "vigorous" which perhaps does something to save the situation.
The only virtue about the suggestion made at that time which might be called a policy is that it had aged for a long time, but I am not at all sure that age is a necessary requisite of an immigration policy although it may be an advantage with other products. We have heard that for some thirty years and so far it has not got us anywhere. Speaking in this house in December, 1949, I said:
I ask this house, by what stretch of the imagination is a nephew 25 years old less desirable as an immigrant than his younger brother of eighteen? He is still excluded, however. Why should we admit a niece, but not a cousin? Why may a single man come in, yet we exclude married couples. I believe these categories are unrealistic. They should be abolished.
And again:
I think the test of admissibility to this country must be twofold. First, is the immigrant a useful citizen; and second, is there someone in Canada who will accept responsibility for him, who will guarantee accommodation and maintenance until he becomes self-supporting. Then, providing they are in good health, physically and ideologically, they should be encouraged to come to Canada to build new lives here.
We have set up a new department, and all of us were happy that that had been done. But there is just one thing that has been left out, a new policy. We expected the Department of Citizenship and Immigration to be an improvement over the old immigration department that was tucked away in the department of mines and resources. Instead in its first statement of policy we find that it hesitates, falters " and stumbles. When it speaks now on immigration it has a hollow sound because its policy at the present time is an echo of the past. Canada's immigration policy over the last thirty years has in fact been a "no immigration" policy. I hope we shall have a better policy in the third quarter of the twentieth century than we have had in the second quarter.
We had better get a new minister.

The minister is doing very well and performing satisfactorily. I have no complaints against him and neither should the opposition. If we do not have a more vigorous policy then we shall be hard put to justify our exclusionary laws both to our own citizens and to the world at large. As has been pointed out by a member of the house, we have in Canada the last great
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration reservoir of land in the western world today. With a larger land area than the United States we have a population one-tenth of that of the United States. Yet our total immigration last year amounted to only 95,000 people. On May 27 the minister spoke before the Kiwanis club, and the Ottawa Journal has the following report with reference thereto:
It was estimated that Canada could absorb approximately 140,000 immigrants yearly into her economy . . .
Shame.
I really do not need any help from the hon. member for Kamloops.
Yes, you do.
No, I am not that hard up. Here are some statistics.
Get a new minister and a new government.
In 1948 the monthly average of immigrants entering Canada was 9,352. In 1949 it was down to 6,966, and in 1950 it was down to 4,823.
And the hon. member for Kamloops got that information for you.

I thought the press party was over. Let me give the committee some interesting statistics with respect to British immigrants. In 1948, 46,000 British immigrants came to Canada, in 1949, 22,000, and in 1950, on the basis of the first three months, only
15,000	will come to this country. The total number of immigrants in 1948 was 125,414, in 1949, 95,215, and in 1950, on the basis of the number that have come to Canada in the first three months, it will be 60,000 at the most. I think that is a very sad picture indeed from our point of view. When we deduct from that the number of people those who have been emigrating to the United States, we realize that our net increase is a pretty insignificant number.
The minister tells us that the policy of the government is to foster the growth of the population of Canada by the encouragement of immigration. My purpose in speaking tonight is to try to build a fire under the minister and the department so that he may get on with his job. One hon. member referred to an article by Sir Norman Angell which appeared in the London Observer. The article pointed out that at the time of Lincoln's death the population of the United States numbered little more than 30 million. Today it is a nation of 150 million people enjoying the highest standard of living in the world. In the fifty years following the civil war the United States has admitted over 33 million immigrants, or almost two and a half times

Supply-Citizenship and Immigration the number of people in Canada today. I think it is well for us to reflect what would have happened to the United States and to the world if her population had remained at 30 million or thereabouts. I doubt very much whether we would have been here today to even talk about this problem.
We in Canada are facing the same challenge in 1950 that the United States faced in 1865. At our present rate of increase our statisticians predict that we will reach a static population of only 18 million by 1980, and that beyond that we can only hope for a decline. I, and I hope other members, will not accept what appears to be the fact that Canada must reach the peak of her development in 1980. Not only our prosperity but our very existence compels us to prove that the statisticians are wrong. There is only one way to prove they are wrong, and that is by more and more immigration of the desirable ' kind. We cannot have an immigration policy based on a tailor-made labour program. I call on the minister to take a leaf out of Australia's book. There is a country with half the population of Canada and only a tiny fraction of our resources. They are taking in 200,000 people a year. I refuse to believe that we cannot absorb any more than 95,000. I think Canada can and must admit a minimum of 200,000 immigrants a year over the next thirty or fifty years. If we do less we are deliberately stunting our growth. If we deliberately fail to build up this country's population then we deserve whatever the consequences may be.
The Minister of Citizenship and Immigration has inherited an able and conscientious department but I ask him not to inherit the old hand-me-down policy as well. It served us badly in the past and it does not look any better for the future. Times have changed with regard to many things, and as to immigration as well. The people of the world are no longer clamouring at our doors to come here in the same way that they used to. Many have grown tired of waiting and have gone to some other place-and I do not mean "the other place", as you well know. It is up to us now to go out and get immigrants, to sell them the idea of coming to Canada in the same way that Australia is doing at the present time. We must have more British immigrants. I have an article from the Windsor Star of June 6, 1950, which reads:
Canada's parliament now is in the last great rush to conclude the business of the present session. It should not be in such a hurry, however, that no attention will be given the problem of immigration from the United Kingdom. In the past, that has been the most important source of immigration. It should be also in the future. But it won't be unless some action is taken to unblock the dam holding
[Mr. Croll.l
back a flow of immigrants, the fact they are unable to bring their money with them due to currency restrictions. Meanwhile, the British are going in great numbers to Australia and New Zealand. This should not be so. It isn't good for Canada or for the commonwealth. The government should devise, if at all possible, some way around this obstacle, and do it this session. Otherwise we will be missing out on some of the most desirable immigrants who will go elsewhere.
According to an article which appeared in the Toronto Star of May 15, a Gallup poll in Great Britain indicated that 48 per cent of the people between the ages of 21 and 29 were prepared to emigrate, and that 41 per cent of those between the ages of 30 and 49 were also prepared to leave that country. Their first choice, of course, is Australia; their second choice is New Zealand, and their third choice is Canada. They are very anxious to come here. In 1949, as I have already indicated, there was a decline of almost 50 per cent in immigration from the British isles as compared with the previous year, and we may expect that decline to continue unless we do something about it and do it now. Britain has been traditionally a source of very good citizens, but at the present time we find them fenced off by currency regulations. Somehow we must break down those barriers; and I am sure if there is the will to do it it can be done. I feel that in future we shall regret our failure to stock this country with more people from the British isles.
Australia is actually subsidizing British immigration. As a matter of fact an immigrant leaving Britain today for Australia can save a thousand dollars, because he has all transportation costs paid for himself and family, while he must pay for his own transportation to this country. It may be that we will have to do the same thing, or work out some method of unfreezing a man's assets in Britain. Perhaps the answer would be for the government to take over a certain proportion of the assets in Britain of a prospective immigrant, and advance him the money in this country. Whatever the solution, we must find it; it is our bounden duty to do so.
There are other countries where we have to go shopping for immigrants. We are doing very well in Holland at the present time, and fairly well in Italy. The Benelux countries are available to us, as well as Norway and Sweden. For almost sixty years we have drawn people from those small countries, and they have helped build up Canada. Today when we consider our position as citizens in this country of Canada, as well as members of the British commonwealth of nations, I believe it is clear to most of us that subtle and insidious indoctrinations emanating from without, and cleverly worked out propaganda from within, are at work today trying to undermine the very foundations of our way of life. I feel confident that we need not be much concerned about the potential forces from without which threaten to destroy us, providing that we as Canadians clearly understand our duties and responsibilities to Canada. With a common unity of purpose to common ideals, come what may we can always face with confidence any threat to our existence. That is where good citizenship plays such an important role. Even if the forces from without which are threatening our existence did not exist, it is only through good citizenship that we can improve the conditions under which we live, and bring happiness and well-being to our people.
The essence of good citizenship is one's love or loyalty to his country, or what is termed patriotism. Patriotism welds all the diversified elements which we have in this country into a hard core of resistance should outside forces not only threaten but challenge us. I think it is fortunate that the genius of the British and American peoples lies in their gift for successfully integrating various stocks, and in making the citizens conscious of their duties and responsibilities to the country in which they live. I say it was for this reason they were able to build up strong nations within the commonwealth, and within the United States. That is why Canada, after the last two world wars, has emerged much more powerful and is able to play a greater role in international affairs; that is why, during the last war, Canadians made a contribution to the war effort which was noble and enduring.
Although we have reason to be proud of our achievement in our unity of purpose, yet I think we must admit that our record of good citizenship is not without blemish. Although we take pride in championing the democratic rights of the individual, yet too often in the past have we found ourselves, or have we seen people, the victims of prejudices. Too often in the past have we found people prejudiced because of a man's colour, or because of the church he attends, or because of his racial origin, or because his name does not sound Anglo-Saxon. It may be Petrosky, or Eisenhower, or pronounced "Yonson" instead of Johnson by his friends. Too often have we seen various clubs refusing the applications of applicants because they were considered to be foreigners or of foreign extraction, although they may have been naturalized in


this country many years ago or may have even been born in this country. Too often in the past have we heard statements made with a certain undertone of contempt when reference was made to a Jew, or a Catholic, or a damn Englishman. I know some choice expressions, Mr. Chairman, about the Scotch and Irish, but I think my better judgment tells me not to use them at this time. At any rate too many people have entertained in their minds a dislike for the unlike. Fortunately this is now becoming past history, and I think we are getting away from that.
I believe our fault was that we were not building a strong Canadian conscience. We were not selling Canadianism to Canadians. During the course of this debate the member for Lake Centre made reference to the difficulty with regard to the census regulations as they existed prior to the passing of the Canadian Citizenship Act. Incidentally, although we may not all agree with everything the member for Lake Centre may say in this chamber, yet I do say that that was one of the finest speeches on citizenship I have ever heard. To those who did not have the good fortune to hear it, I would suggest that they read it in Hansard. In any event he pointed out the difficulty that existed with reference to the census regulations prior to the passing of the citizenship act. That is why I feel that the Canadian Citizenship Act was one of the greatest pieces of legislation ever enacted by this parliament. Under it, regardless of our racial origin, regardless of what church we may attend, regardless of what occupation we may follow, one thing we have in common with our fellow Canadians is Canadian citizenship. At the same time we remain as members of the British commonwealth of nations, and retain our status in that great organization which I believe is the greatest organization the world has ever seen.
After the last war considerably over a quarter of a million immigrants came to Canada from various parts of the world. I should like to speak particularly of those people who came from continental Europe, many of whom were formerly in displaced persons camps. The interesting question arises, what do those newcomers expect and hope for in Canadian life? What do we, as Canadians, expect from them? Are we to regard the newcomer as a queer individual with a name that is hard to pronounce, unable to speak English, and leave him to his own devices; or do we as Canadians have a duty and obligation to those people? I believe all hon. members will agree with me that, no matter where one goes, people's wants and desires are similar. The newcomer's desires may be

summed up as follows: First, he wants to learn the language. Second, he wants economic security. Third, he wants to be accepted socially in the community in which he resides. To the newcomer the language is of the utmost importance. If he is to obtain and retain a job; if he is to follow or understand instructions from his employers; if he is to get along with his associates, he must know the language. If he is to know what is taking place in the world, he must read the newspapers and follow what is being said on the radio.
I have had occasion to personally interview many of these newcomers. One of the first things they set about learning is the language. I must say that I was pleasantly surprised in finding many of them have made progress in learning the language of this country. Economic security is also a major desire on the part of the newcomer. After having spent years in concentration camps or displaced persons camps he wishes to find a job, to do some work, which will give him and his family a fairly happy surrounding and a decent home life. Only by their achieving this can one expect those newcomers to retain their self-respect.
The third desire, namely, social acceptance in a community, is such that the newcomer wants to be on an equal footing with his fellow citizens. This probably is the most important factor in developing in him a love for the country which he has adopted as his own.
In general, a newcomer has a feeling that he will not only enjoy the privileges of his newly adopted land, but be able to do his share in contributing to his community and to the Canadian national life.
We, on the other hand, want people with new skills and new devices for the development of our natural resources, and who will supply us not only with unskilled but also with skilled labour, who will increase our national income, and who will help to defend this country should the need arise. 1 believe that probably the strongest defence program that we could have for this country of ours is by getting more people into this country, although I do not intend to dwell on the question of immigration at this time. In any event we want immigrants who, when they come into this country, will become good Canadians.

25,000	or 30,000 people a year going or coming from one country to another. In accepting a certain movement of immigrants I think my stand is still reasonable. I ask the minister to give strong orders to his officials so that they will carefully screen immigrants coming to Canada. I believe our experience has been costly enough that we should not forget that side of the situation.
The confederation was answering, as were many others in French Canada, the appeal of Pius XII on behalf of displaced persons and orphans. This appeal has been underlined by Monseigneur Charbonneau, former bishop of Montreal, as reported by I'Action Catholique in August, 1947. If one reads carefully the speech of Senator Gouin at McMaster university-and I commend it to every member of the house-
And of the Senate too.

And of the Senate too-he will have a picture of the views on immigration policy expressed in the province of Quebec, a picture starting from the nineties and carrying on up till now. He will see that in the province of Quebec there are radical expressions of opinion as to immigration, and at the same time there are very reasonable and intelligent considerations of the subject.
No one could blame my French compatriots for showing a preference for French, Belgian, Dutch or Italian immigration. I was pleased to hear the hon. member who spoke before me ask for Italian immigration. I am always glad to hear that people like immigrants of Italian extraction. I am in favour of that to some extent. No one can blame my French compatriots for asking for Belgian or French immigrants. In doing so they simply follow the same path as other provinces in asking for immigrants from the British isles. There is nothing wrong about that on either side. It is quite natural. I have certain figures which I secured from the department in 1948. It is surprising to find that if Ontario, for example, shows a preference for British

In reading these figures very carefully we can see that Quebec has not been receiving such a large number of French, Italian or Belgian immigrants. In 1948 Ontario received four times as many Belgians as Quebec, and over ten times as many Dutch. La Terre de Chez-Nous, a French periodical issued by the Union Catholique des Cultivateurs, of Quebec had this to say in the issue of November 5, 1948. I do not read this in any critical sense, but merely to show the picture in Quebec province, because I believe the article gives a good resume of the whole question. It was written after the announcement that French immigrants were to be on the same footing as Britishers. The article said:
(Translation):
It is not enough to have fairer immigration regulations. They must also be put to good use. Immigrants from France have access to our country just like those from England and the United States. Many French people wish to settle in Canada. This contribution from the mother country could be useful to us in a thousand ways. Here, however, the provincial authorities or some private organization would have to be willing to take care of them. What has been done in this respect? Silence is the only answer . . .
Again, in La terre de chez nous, one can read in the report of an inquiry conducted for Le Devoir by Mr. Frangois Zalloni:
One wonders, finally, if now we will see the province of Quebec admit French immigrants in as large a number as the group of British people welcomed to Ontario. Observers feel that it is up to Mr. Duplessis and the industrialists of this province.
If British immigrants settled in great numbers in the neighbouring province, it is due to the fact that, first of all, Premier Drew went and fetched them in Great Britain and that, with the agreement of Ontario employers, he opened a provincial employment bureau for immigrants in London.
If we want the French to settle here, our government and our businessmen should do likewise. If we feel that recent immigration from Britain disrupts the ethnical balance of our country, the remedy lies, after all, in our own hands.
(Text):
I hope there will be no misunderstanding of my position on this matter. I simply wish to give the complete picture, and to show the different opinions that have been expressed in my province by different newspapers. In every expression of opinion can be detected the desire that the best possible choice be made, that the best methods be followed and that reasonable consideration be given to

such matters as mentality, way of life and way of thinking. I believe that is the right angle from which one must approach the question.
After these citizens are here it is our duty to show them that despite diversity of religion, language and tradition, Canada is proceeding toward complete unity of action. In Mr. Zalloni's report one perceives the lack of any organization to bring good and assimilable immigrants to Quebec. Here is a report from Relations of January, 1950:
(Translation):
We are not the ones who acknowledge these facts, who compare, proclaim and applaud; it is Maclean's magazine of December 15:
Relations quotes Maclean's magazine:
According to Premier Frost, the population of Ontario increases by 10,000 people a month and now exceeds four and a half million. The largest of our provinces keeps its lead; Quebec has less than 4 million people and its population increases by only 8,000 a month.
Autonomy allows others, smarter than we, to bring in reinforcements, tens of thousands of refugees, especially British or Dutch, who are well established on farms. The Pope has asked countries with vast territories to receive those who have none left, since that is better than almsgiving. Will. Quebec therefore continually refuse to open its doors, its barricaded territories, even to our own kin?
(Text):
This quotation shows once more that prominent people of Quebec are ready to help these unhappy people find a new country and build a better life, and to deplore the ineptitude and indifference in some quarters in facing the situation intelligently and in a spirit of Christian charity. Not long ago the Gazette gave the views of prominent French newspapers in our province. The first was Le Canada:
The era of mass immigration to Canada has come to an end because the conditions that inspired it are no longer in force . . . but from the simple point of humanitarianism we cannot close our doors to foreigners who seek to establish themselves here. This does not mean we should accept anybody whatsoever, but we should exercise a judicious choice. Nor is the question of offering a welcome to these new Canadians something we should longer neglect. It is our duty to initiate them into the way Canadians live and to facilitate their assimilation. The new Minister of Immigration has a full enough program facing him and he will be able doubtlessly to rise to the heights of his task.
Then Le Droit had this to say:
It is to be regretted that similar steps are not being taken in Quebec as in Ontario to increase the population . . . There are not only Frenchmen, Italians and Belgians whom we could settle in Quebec. We are assured that it would be advantageous to welcome those Dutch Catholics who are desirous of settling in our country.
Do and say as we like, Canada will always receive immigrants, and if we do not make use of them for ourselves they will be made use of against us.

As you see, this newspaper speaks very frankly.
If Quebec had shown any vision, it would, during the last fifty years, have practised an intelligent policy in regard to population. This province does not lack wealth. It lacks only strong arms to exploit it.
Then Le Soleil:
It is impossible to oppose all immigration in principle, provided that it be reasonable, in good order, well selected and in no way directed against one of the two principal elements of the Canadian population. This is what our representatives in the Commons must say when the opportunity arises and they must demand a guarantee that immigration must be kept within fair limits if recruiting begins again.
I could give many other quotations to prove once more that it should be the care of everyone to maintain a fair balance between provinces, and at the same time get immigrants particularly likely to be assimilated in this or that region. And we must also be careful in our choice and screening abroad. I believe we had our lesson in the past. Without discriminating against any race or religion, it is our privilege to bring here only those whose political philosophy is not opposed to ours. Too often in the past-and I do not reproach anyone-have we received in good faith people who themselves were not frank and have not been grateful to Canada for the marvellous hospitality granted them.
The communist fifth column is always in action, and takes every possible means of increasing its effective number and efficiency in action. Everyone recalls the lottery which, international in scope, was discovered in Montreal before the Italian election. Its purpose was to provide funds for the Italian communists. The first prize was a thirty-day trip to Moscow. This lottery would have had no chance of success if its sponosors could not count on the activity of new immigrants. These people must have been well informed, because they knew where to go. Within our time we have had the declaration of Lieutenant General W. Anders, wartime Polish army leader, which reads as follows:
Communist agents disguised as refugees are entering Canada.
In a letter to Mr. MacNamara, deputy minister of labour, as reprinted in the Toronto Star of May 1, General Anders added:
Insufficiently screened persons are coming to Canada among Polish refugees and are creating ill feeling towards Polish immigrants as a whole.
I know personally that extreme caution has been the motto of both the departments of labour and immigration in the screening of immigrants. It would be impossible to create an air-tight wall against every undesirable entry. No nation can praise herself

Supply-Citizenship and Immigration for never having been deceived in that connection. But with strict orders and attention every minute, we can diminish the number of those whose patriotism does not even extend to the country of their adoption but to only one sovereignty, and I need not mention it by name. The question is not how many thousands of immigrants we are going to bring, but how many good immigrants are we going to accept? How many are fit to accept our way of living, our views on the democratic way of life? How many can be assimilated, and in what regions? It has been the experience in some districts, a somewhat costly experience, that many of those we have received have been a burden, and a source of trouble. Many have forgotten the manner in which we received them, and the welcome that was extended to them. They have turned their activities against the land of their adoption, and tried to sabotage our institutions. Let us not be too confident. Let the officials of the department be more and more cautious. The choice must be judicious, and the screening parsimonious.
Let me repeat the advice of Miss Betty B. Robinson:
It is better to be overcautious than to be reckless in the matter of immigration.
If perchance someone cheats the screening, at the first sign of anti-Canadian activities he should be sent back where he belongs.

Mr. Chairman, it is timely to pay a tribute to the hon. member for Port-neuf for his industry in compiling such data on immigration. He and the hon. member for Spadina are both specialists in immigration. They hold divergent views, and this illustrates the difficult task of the minister in deciding the issue. One thing struck me in the speech of the member for Portneuf. It was his contention that communism is a religion. If I read the dictionary I see that religion is the practice of sacred rights; one of the prevalent systems of faith and worship; human recognition of a superhuman controlling power, and especially of a personal God entitled to obedience; the effect of such recognition on the mental attitude, et cetera.
I do not understand how an atheist can be a religious man, but perhaps the communists are worshipping Stalin. He may be their god. In that connection they must be considered rather as pagans, but the pagans are religious too. What I cannot understand is how an atheist can be a religious man.
I can explain it to the hon. member if he wishes.
Yes.

When you want to destroy the notion of God you have to develop a philosophy, or what I call a religion, to destroy the notion of God. You have to form what I call the anti-God religion, and that is what communism has done in the world. If my hon. friend will look more closely into communism, he will see that they have their god in Stalin. They have their thirteen apostles in the politburo. They have all the pictures of their saints and their god everywhere in the country. That is why I say it is a religion.

I appreciate what my hon. friend has said, but a religion is necessarily something positive, while atheism is the negation of a positive act, that of worshipping God or a superhuman being. I will tell my hon. friend that I am not a doctor of divinity, so I shall not proceed further with the matter.

They worship
matter, materialism.

They worship the cinders of Lenin. I will tell you, sir, that it is very important to have men in this country to defend the people in a spiritual matter, in a religion that is in accordance with the statute passed a hundred years ago by the upper and lower provinces of Canada. This statute concerned the freedom of worship, and has been incorporated in the statutes of the province of Quebec and the province of Ontario. It is to the effect that we have freedom of religion in this country provided that the practice of this religion is not against the established order of this country. It is for this reason that the way the Doukhobors worship is not acceptable to us, and why there are punishments in their case.
It is most important to bring men from other countries who are worthy of being Canadians; whatever is their belief; whatever their race, provided they decide to become Canadians and consider this country as the country of their adoption just as the missionaries did in the early history of the colony. There was Monseigneur de Laval, the first bishop of Quebec, who belonged to one of the finest families in France. There was Monseigneur de Saint-Vallier, who was a chaplain in France. These men came to preach the gospel amongst the Indians. They sacrificed all the advantages and benefits they might had had in the old country, and came here to civilize the new world. They were true Canadians. They were French by birth but they were Canadians by spirit, and that is the type of men and women we want in this country.
